item.title: Final Fantasy 7 Revelation will let players access Hard Mode from the very beginning of the journey, unlike FF7 Remake and Rebirth, which made folks roll credits before unlocking the tougher difficulty option. Read more
item.description:
Final Fantasy 7 Revelation will let players access Hard Mode from the very beginning of the journey, unlike FF7 Remake and Rebirth, which made folks roll credits before unlocking the tougher difficulty option.
The tidbit comes courtesy of director Naoki Hamaguchi, who told Hardcore Gamer that Final Fantasy 7 Revelation's Hard Mode "won't function in the exact same way" as it did previously. For next year's third and final chapter, the team "reimagined the high-difficulty experience to align with the new game design."
You see, this time around, the world of Gaia supposedly opens up really early in the game. Cloud and company can fly straight to some of the game's toughest battles as soon as they jump into their flying airship, whether they're ready for the fight or not, so Square Enix's approach to difficulty had to change too.
"Hard Mode is selectable from the very start of this game," Hamaguchi explained. "Therefore, players who want to tackle challenging battles and high-difficulty gameplay right from the beginning can enjoy that experience from their very first playthrough. This is because, unlike Remake and Rebirth, Revelation offers a wide variety of end-game content even after you've beaten the game. Rather than relying solely on the traditional flow of challenging Hard Mode after beating the game, we aimed to create a game where players can enjoy various new content and challenges even after completing the main story."
As much as I loved both Remake and Rebirth, the combat never properly pushed me to my limits and tested my creaky reflexes until I finally reached that second playthrough - in the case of Rebirth, that meant playing the game for at least 50 hours. FF7 Revelation is shaping up to be another behemoth that could easily take 100 hours to fully complete, apparently, so I'm very relieved to hear that I can get to the good stuff from the jump. Hard Mode is truly where these games shine.
In a separate tweet, Hamaguchi also shared there'll be a Dynamic Mode at launch, like in Rebirth, "allowing players to enjoy consistently challenging battles throughout the game." It also looks like we'll be able to adjust how tricky those many, many mini-games are. (Damn you, Moogles!)
Final Fantasy 7 Revelation is coming to PC, PS5, Nintendo Switch 2 and Xbox Series X/S on 8th April, 2027.

item.title: Arc Raiders is still going strong almost a year after finding viral success, and it's all thanks to Embark Studios' one-two-punch strategy of launching a huge new update, Frozen Trails, to coincide with a free weekend. Read more
item.description:
Arc Raiders is still going strong almost a year after finding viral success, and it's all thanks to Embark Studios' one-two-punch strategy of launching a huge new update, Frozen Trails, to coincide with a free weekend.
Arc Raiders' Frozen Trails update upgraded the extraction shooter to version 2.0 earlier this month - 8th October - and quickly led to a surge in Steam players interested in its tense PvEvP shootouts. A new report from Alinea Analytics' Rhys Elliott now claims a similar resurgence took place across all platforms where the game's available.
According to the report, Arc Raiders' comeback peaked with a whopping 1.7m daily players jumping in on the 14th of October, its biggest player count in six months, mostly driven by the aforementioned update. What's perhaps most interesting is that player numbers actually peaked just after the game's free trial weekend ended on 12th October - though around 150,000 new looters reportedly joined the robo-infested wasteland during that weekend period.
Both events coincided with the game's steepest discount yet, slashing its price tag by 50% to $19.99. In the three days after the free trial, Arc Raiders sold another 150,000 copies and brought home roughly $3m, not counting microtransactions, per the report.
Embark Studios' seemingly went all out this month. Frozen Trails itself nudged almost every corner of the game, adding a new map, new weapons, new menacing mechs and much more.
A PvE test also tried to accommodate the game's surprisingly friendly community between the 13th and 20th of October. Executive producer Aleksander Grøndal recently said the team isn't against the idea of permanently splitting Arc Raiders' PvEvP gameplay into PvE and PvP pockets. Who knows? Doing so could open the door to another resurgence if done well.
Earlier this month, we learned the production company behind this summer's big screen horror hit, Backrooms, is working to adapt both Arc Raiders and The Finals into film and TV projects. Developer Embark is involved, too.

item.description:
Ken Kutaragi, the founder of PlayStation and architect of the first three PlayStation consoles, has said that people being upset about Sony's discontinuation of game discs is probably a "mentality issue". He understands it, he noted, but that doesn't make it "economically reasonable" for Sony to keep printing them.
Kutaragi was speaking to Video Games Chronicle at the Game Republic New Horizons event, where he said: "I understand that physical discs have become a metaphor for 'owning' games. I really understand that mentality... But nobody thinks [physical media] is necessary for a networked device like a smartphone, for example, because people feel that they will keep their content. So it's a mentality.
"I really understand [why some people are upset]," he added, "but I don't think it's economically reasonable. Maybe it's a mentality issue."
Kutaragi retired from PlayStation in June 2007, shortly after the PlayStation 3's European release, so he's been out of the company for a while. Two generations of consoles have passed since he left, though I'm sure he has close ties to Sony and people working there still. "I'm not the CEO at PlayStation any more," he noted in the interview, "but we still have some common [view points]."
Maybe Sony is pushing towards an all-digital device, he remarked, in a similar way that we see smartphones and other devices. "Maybe that's how those people are thinking," he said. "But this has caused some friction with game enthusiasts."
Kutaragi's advice? Harness AI and cloud computing to their full potential and "we won't need any console". I don't think that'll go down terribly well, Ken.

item.title: The Japan Actors Union has issued new rules, guidelines, and restrictions related to AI-generated voice use. This includes an outright ban on the replication of the voices of dead actors, unless the actor had authorised its use during their lifetime. Read more
item.description:
The Japan Actors Union has issued new rules, guidelines, and restrictions related to AI-generated voice use. This includes an outright ban on the replication of the voices of dead actors, unless the actor had authorised its use during their lifetime.
Per Automaton, these guidelines are meant to protect an industry that has been exposed to exploitation by generative AI. One example includes voice actor Kenjiro Tsuda (Jujutsu Kaisen and Chainsaw Man) taking Tiktok to court in an attempt to remove AI-generated voice imitations from the platform. He would go on to lose that case, but not without setting a precedent that a person's voice is subject to protection under publicity rights laws.
The guidelines cover four major points. The first is focused on consent and establishes that permission must be granted at "every stage" of the generative AI process. This would mean AI companies require permission from actors before models are trained on their performances.
The second point, meanwhile, states that AI replications of an actor's work are to be counted as a new performance under the guidelines. This would mean royalties or compensation must be paid by AI companies to the actors involved.
Next up comes generative AI-powered translations, which takes an actor's performance and automatically changes it to another language. These must maintain the "artistic integrity" of the original performance, the guidelines state, and may not be used without permission in overseas regions.
"The Japan Actors Union will strive to not just establish these guidelines as industry-wide rules, but also strengthen its efforts to encourage the government to legislate regulations that protect 'voice rights'," wrote The Japan Actors Union (translated by Automaton). "Technological advancements will not stop, but the 'living, breathing human expression' and a 'respect for rights' must always remain at its core."
It is worth noting that these guidelines are not laws and therefore are not binding rules AI companies must follow. Even so, it marks a major push from the Japan Actors Union for this to change. These new guidelines contribute to mounting pressure against the generative AI industry in Japan, as actors continue to push for better protections.
Japan's Voice Actor Union is not the only one pushing back against generative AI. In Western countries, similar collectives have been speaking out about the technologies' impact on the field, with one describing it as "catastrophic".

item.title: Bullet-dodging PlayStation shooter Saros has welcomed a sizeable Zenith update today, which has the twin aims of making the game both more accessible for those who haven't played it (or are struggling to get into it) and more replayable for those who have. Read more
item.description:
Bullet-dodging PlayStation shooter Saros has welcomed a sizeable Zenith update today, which has the twin aims of making the game both more accessible for those who haven't played it (or are struggling to get into it) and more replayable for those who have.
The headline additions are a quickfire boss-rush mode, a New Game Plus mode, an entire new layer of modifiers to make runs easier and harder, and - very appealingly - a slow-mo option to slow the game down.
The Slow Game Speed option can be varied depending on preference and can be activated either manually or automatically. You choose how much it slows the game down by; a video of it makes it look a lot like slow-mo in many other games, providing crucial thinking time in Saros you otherwise struggle to get.
Developer Housemarque said in a blog post it was "always wary" about toning down its games. "Although we realise our games can look intimidating at first, we didn’t want to compromise the combat system of Saros by reducing the projectiles that put the 'bullet' in 'bullet ballet'," it said. Hence the new slow game speed.
The new game modifiers allow you to tune the difficulty depending on what kind of challenge you're up for. If you want a bit of help, there are 10 new Protection modifiers you can apply. An example given was of a Corruption Melee Enhancement, which unleashes the game's deadly Corruption that builds up on you for huge melee damage.
Meanwhile, if you want to make the game harder, there are Trial modifiers. An example given was of Hostile Regeneration, which allows crowd-controlled enemies to quickly regain health unless you close to melee and finish them off with a strike.
The New Game Plus mode is called Eclipse Layers, and it activates once you've cleared the game. Each new Eclipse Layer represents a more intense version of the game with altered rules, apparently, and each has various prerequisites required in unlocking it; some require a certain amount of modifiers to be in effect, for example.
In step with this, Arjun now wears a cool sun-like crown during the Eclipse Layers - and his armour glows golden - that grows depending on the modifiers you have in play. The crown is also essential for seeing 12 new story visions Housemarque has added to the game for you to find.
Finally, Overlord Rush is the boss-rush mode that's designed to be played in 10-minute bursts, giving you a 'set' of the game's bosses to fight. A final set - Totality, it's called - has you face all eight Overlords in one continuous gauntlet.
Saros released in April on PS5 and was well reviewed, though it had a sluggish start in terms of sales, especially compared to predecessor of sorts, Returnal. Housemarque doesn't seem concerned, though, saying "this is just the start of the discussion", and that there's plenty to "tweak and add" and work will continue for "a while". This Zenith update is presumably a major part of that work.

item.description:
This year has seen two highly-rated and beloved Star Wars games in the XCOM-like Zero Company, and the Burnout-like Galactic Racer. And both were made by independent studios rather than much bigger companies, which have typically taken on Star Wars games in recent years, such as Ubisoft with Star Wars Outlaws and EA with Star Wars Battlefront.
The change, it turns out, was intentional. Lucasfilm Games bigwig Douglas Reilly told The Game Business that the Star Wars franchise stewards are now much more open about who to give the license to.
"We're obviously a licensing business," Reilly explained, "so we're not the publishers any more of products. Our goal is to try and find a publishing partner and a developer or a publisher and a developer. I think we've tried to be more flexible about who we're willing to take pitches from. Good ideas can come from a lot of different places."
This is a fairly recent change in Lucasfilm Games' strategy. The license holder was previously happy to sell a single publisher exclusive rights to Star Wars games, which previously was EA. That approach has often been criticised for limiting the creative output, be it in the number of games released or genres that get chosen. That dearth is something Star Wars fans truly felt when EA had exclusive rights to Star Wars, but this new approach allows for a much more varied pool of games and more frequent releases.
To that end, Reilly revealed there is no particular tier of publisher that Lucasfilm Games targets, saying, "There are some hurdles; we have a high quality bar and we want to make sure they're excellent experiences. And that means typically you work with more experienced teams than new teams." However, that doesn't mean you "necessarily [have to] be a top-five publisher to make a great Star Wars game".
Reilly also teased what we can expect from Star Wars games in the future. "We're exploring all kinds of things, large and small," he said, "with partners that I think are going to continue to surprise folks who are like, 'Oh, they're doing a thing with them. That might be interesting to see how that turns out.'"
The number of currently announced Star Wars games remains small. Outside of Quantic Dream's long-in-development Star Wars Eclipse, the only other game that's understood to be in the works is the third game in Respawn's Star Wars Jedi series. Former Mass Effect and Knights of the Old Republic lead Casey Hudson is currently working on a follow-up, Fate of the Old Republic, as Saber Interactive continues to insist the Knights of the Old Republic Remake remains in development.

item.description:
It took me longer than I'd like to admit to realise something obvious about Star Wars Zero Company. The fate of its eponymous crew - short of cash, betrayed by the shifting sands of circumstance in a tumultuous wider world, scrambling to just about get the job over the line - is really a lot like that of its developers at Bit Reactor. Furloughed for about a month before the game was released, those staff have clearly hustled and scrapped and fought to the last. And so Zero Company the game bears the signs of its development. In places it feels a little patched together, a little under-ready, a game that launched into the world like a roguish pilot might launch a half-repaired starfighter. The windscreen's rattling, warning lights are flashing, one particularly hirsute engineer is deeply unimpressed at the decision to take off, and nobody knows where that ominous groaning noise is coming from. But somehow she's up. And in the end that's all that counts.
Zero Company is not a tidy game, then - truly, I've a list of nitpicks longer than this review - but it is also a bit of a gem. There's so much love here. At times it borders on the saccarine, some characters getting a little too wistful, moments of crewmate dialogue a little too breathy, too aww, shucks. But I've an enduring soft spot for games where you can feel the development of it as you play. And it's more than just the slightly taped-together vibes that give Zero Company that impression here. You can feel the development of this game because you can feel the thinking behind it. The many hours that years-long experts of turn-based tactics (many Bit Reactor devs have pedigree at Firaxis, developer of the modern XCOM games) have spent sat in, I'd like to imagine, a big, comfortable chair. Perhaps with their feet resting, legs crossed, up on their desk. And staring intently at the ceiling until the solution to one design problem or another presented itself. A game I imagine as being developed much the same as it's played.
A nice twist, however, is in how relaxed that playing can be. Zero Company's default difficulty is on the easy side, pitched at newcomers to the turn-based tactical genre, and in turn it makes for a perfect match to the source material. Star Wars Zero Company is set in the late Clone Wars era - roughly parallel to Episode 3, in other words - which also happens to be the prime kids TV era. This is the time when Obi Wan Kenobi was a cool action figure warrior-general with big shoulder pads and there were lots of Trooper dudes with names like Rex diving around shooting their lasers. It's also the period that plays home to Andor, the gloriously realised political melodrama about revolution, solidarity, and the banality of evil under fascism, perched right at the opposite end of the Star Wars Seriousness Spectrum. And so Zero Company has these two, ostensibly opposing threads running through it, tasking it with somehow tying together light entertainment and timely introspection. And somehow, it does it quite well.
The default difficulty is part of the reason why (though there are hard and ironman-like modes for the true tacticos and sickos out there, of course). There's a novelty to angling a game in this genre - a genre more often associated with those iron men - at the casual crowd, in aiming for breeziness and satisfaction first. This is my first time enjoying one of these games as a good old-fashioned romp, where there might be the occasional grabbing of a hat beneath the closing door but, broadly speaking, you will find yourself playing as the good guys who ultimately always come out on top.
That pairs nicely with Zero Company's take on telling a story. Rather than the XCOM approach of an aggressively replayable campaign with a feather-light narrative layer, Zero Company has a proper beginning-middle-end story. This is where the Andor side of things comes in. Zero Company is far from that level of writing and execution, unfortunately, and perhaps expectedly. It relays its themes broadly and a little clunkily, falling into familiar video game traps that so often feel unavoidable because of the way the game itself is structured.
Characters, for instance, often need to deliver entire backstories in a couple of throwaway lines - lines which most players might never hear because they didn't opt to talk to the right static NPC between the right missions. Or which they might hear a variation of multiple times because they talked to them at every opportunity, and developers need to make sure those skip-lots-of-conversations players get their required minimum exposition to know what's going on. There's also a lot of overly-breathy voice work - Jae, who has a moderately interesting background as a kind of ore-baron nepo baby who wants to do good, is a particular culprit of the kind of over-earnestness that can jar just a little.
The truth is a lot of Star Wars media is always going to struggle to execute its themes with the sophistication we now know to be possible, post-Andor. But what helps Zero Company is that those themes are at least there, and more than that, they're both fully understood and delivered with heartfelt sincerity. There's a wonderful transition, which I'll try not to spoil, where this crew's story shifts from underdog adventure-romp (that's the third of Star Wars' three pillars accounted for: original trilogy ruffian-camp), through Clone Wars action melodrama, and out the other side into something about bigger ideas. I only wish it had gone on for a little longer after that point - you'll know it when you play it - to give that final part a bit more time to breathe.
All that said, I expect most people coming to Zero Company are coming because you can conveniently shorten it to ZCOM. This is a tactics game from tactics virtuosos, ultimately, and in the playing is where it really shows. The big twist for XCOM fans is the removal of the two-action limit. Here you get three, though rather than that simply feeling like action point creep - like before, but more! - it's another decision I can feel the armchair thinking in. The genius of two is the simplicity, and the tension that comes from it. Move and shoot, or move further? By moving to three action points - but, crucially, in doing so making some actions cost one point, some two, some three or all the points you have left - you introduce a new kind of tension. Now it matters even more which character shoots first, and at whom.
An example: Trick, a trusty ex-Republic trooper, has an automatic 'repeater' blaster that, when used, consumes all his remaining action points, doing more damage the more he has left to spend. This means he can only ever shoot at one enemy per turn, but also that he can do a lot of damage to that one enemy if he stays still. Or he can move quite far - two thirds of the maximum range - and still do a little damage at the end. Now you have an interesting choice to make: do you make Trick a single-target nuke for taking chunks of HP out of elites? Or do you send him off on quests to pick off puny, dead-in-one-shot battle droids? Over the course of a single battle he could be both.
All this is instantly more sophisticated when you add in each character's various abilities - both passive and active - and items. I opted for my delightfully customisable main character, Hawkes, to be a sharpshooter, giving him a sniper rifle and some excellent sniper-related skills. He can zero in, gaining a load of stacks of lethality - critical chance, accuracy - in exchange for one of his three points. That sniper rifle takes the remaining two to fire, and all those stacks are lost if he moves or is otherwise rudely displaced. He, like all named characters, also comes with a few unique aspects too, such as being able to give another ally an extra action point, and providing a couple passive buffs.
Those active abilities require you to spend a resource called Advantage, which builds up as you land hits on enemies through the course of an encounter, up to a maximum of 10. At harder difficulties or in tougher encounters this quickly becomes part of your planning: I want to use this ability, but am a little short of Advantage. Do I instead just do something else with that character, or do I use another character to land some hits, build up the Advantage, and go with my original plan? Then the synergies start to kick in.
Cly Kullervo, for instance, has low-cost abilities such as her hugely helpful jetpack, and an electric dart you ideally want to stack up en masse, before triggering one huge, multiplying explosion. That already works nicely with her pistol, which can be fired three times for three Advantage-building hits, but it's even better if you have another character like, say, Tel-Rea Vokoss. As a Jedi Padawan (smartly introduced as a real novice, to keep her deftly balanced), she can push and pull enemies around repeatedly and into one another - both for racking up multiple hits and, if you're clever, disposing of tougher foes in one hit for a bit of good old-fashioned lobbing off the edge of the map. By the end I often found myself using those two, plus Kabb Uppercut, built as an attention-drawing tank, for their excellent dovetailing kits.
But then Jae, for all her sins, has an extremely useful execution ability that picks off an enemy left on low health from almost anywhere on the map. You can work that in with one of Zero Company's other great additions, Assists, for some lovely chain reactions. Each turn, one of your operators gets the option to call for another operator who'll take a free shot at the next enemy the first operator attacks. More than once I found myself nodding proudly at my own late night reflection in the PC monitor, after triggering a chain of attack, assist, execution. Or better yet, you could use an ability to make an operator such as Kabb retaliate after getting a hit. So Kabb could, in theory, call for an assist, shoot an enemy that retaliates, have his ally shoot them for the assist, then get shot by them, then retaliate, then have Jae relieve them of their final chunk of HP from halfway across the map. You could use an ability that lets Kabb assist the next ally who attacks. You could build him so he does lots of extra assist damage. On and on.
The missions themselves are, broadly speaking, enjoyable enough. There are a couple of standouts - escaping along a long bridge that's being blown up behind you is good fun, as are a couple of similarly dynamic missions right towards the end of the story. A few too many follow a slightly rote format of going in and rescuing a temporary extra party member, activating a button, or standing in a zone, although these are the ones that get a fair bit more enjoyable when the challenge is higher.
These are also, typically, the more optional missions, which is where the other half of Zero Company comes in. Like so many others in the genre, there's an element of base management to be overseen between the missions themselves. This time, in what feels like a nod to another Firaxis game in Marvel's Midnight Suns, that base is a physical space you can run around in third-person. This is where those largely static NPCs loiter, your crewmates waiting to pop out a little exposition or mission-by-mission character development on request. At times they are actually quite lovely - I will forever love Kabb's strangely endearing cockney-like dialect, where he seems to speak entirely in rhymey-timey versions of the types of idioms I have spent my life aggressively editing out of video game reviews.
Specific places in your base also act as the various necessary upgrade stations. Each character has a skill tree - later upgraded into two skill trees, the second offering a choice of any character class, which is a nice twist. These are a relatively light touch, some upgrades doing the classic plus-some-percent-crit-chance that can slide under the radar somewhat. But many, even with minor improvements, have a subtly important impact. Upgrading a skill all the way to the end of the tree just to take it from two Advantage points cost to one sounds minor, but can make all the difference in a tight encounter. And those crit chances can, at least, be built up to really significant levels, where with the right play there's a good chance of a crit on almost every shot taken.
Slightly less effective are the Black Market store and the upgrades to the base itself. Both of these were, in my experience, just too expensive to actually implement to the point of making a meaningful difference. On standard difficulty I bought maybe one item in my entire run, the rest being earned as rewards or from various other upgrades (all of this with in-universe credits earned from completing missions, to be clear). Likewise with the base upgrades: the rewards from missions mean you can afford to take roughly one upgrade per 'cycle', with each upgrade typically taking one or two cycles to complete, and you later being able to do two or three upgrades at a time. All of which is to say: you just upgrade them one at a time, with little meaningful choice or strategy to the approach because you simply can't afford to do anything else.
There's a similarly light touch to Operations, a kind of mini-mission system that you must go through each cycle before you undertake that cycle's one mission. These are FTL-like choice-based, text-only scenarios - sometimes dilemmas, sometimes a choice of three equally okay rewards - that can also occasionally impact your bond with crewmates. In being text-only and largely very short and simple, they felt a smidge underrealised, almost as though the third-person view, only used around the base and in introductory snippets of main story missions, originally existed as the vehicle through which you'd be doing these operations instead, only to be cut back at some point along the way.
Bit Reactor could also have skipped the third-person sections of missions themselves. These are brief interludes or prologues to the main story missions themselves, and often little more than a case of jogging in a straight line and scanning two things when prompted. They feel like a legacy of a game with a bit more ambition than it could afford. Perhaps with another six months in the oven - with its staff having not been furloughed before the game even arrived - they'd have been cut, smartly papered over and worked around; us players never knowing they'd even existed. This is what I mean by Zero Company being a game that seems to wear its development in the open.
Lastly on the limitations front, those inter-character bonds, too, feel a little too easy to ignore. Increasing your bond with a character - by taking them on missions, doing assists with them, making Operations decisions they agree with - gives a kind of XP boost to your bond. After enough XP your Bond levels up, then you get a choice of three bonuses for both characters. The motivation then is to increase the bond through the thresholds but, as far as I could gather, that's about the only benefit, and so in the end they feel like a kind of background bonus to simply playing the game over time, rather than with any specific intentionality behind it.
These systems do, though, provide a kind of colour and texture to Zero Company that still has merit in its own right. They're layers. Most of them, on their own, can feel a little lightweight, but combined they still mesh together nicely. What Zero Company does so well is to always give you a decision to make, always a pathway to optimise, an option to prioritise. These management layers work so well over turn-based tactics games because fundamentally they're tapping into that same part of the brain: how can I best allocate my very limited resources with all the information at hand? What are tactics, after all, if not a test of maximising efficiency in a series of individual moments; a part of a strategy that tests your ability to then find that efficiency consistently over time?
This is the magic with Zero Company, ultimately. There are brilliant revisions to the formula here that add nuance and tension and decision points, layering on complexity without complication. There are wonderful moments of theming and tone: through one of Star Wars' richest moments in time, through some deeply likeable characters, and through the old chestnut of emergent storytelling too, as you scramble to get your no-name Glupp Shitto-alike out of one particularly hairy mission alive. And there's depth here if you wish to mine for it. But above all it's just another example of an endlessly winning formula. Of action figures, cartoons, dramas, chessboards, and bottomless pits you can drop bad guys into, with all the glorious, goofball sounds and sights that Star Wars can slather over the top. And on top of all that, it's a game with its developers' earnest effort bursting through it at every opportunity. It's not perfect. It's also just impossible not to love.
A copy of Star Wars Zero Company was provided for this review by EA.

item.title: CD Projekt Red is currently rolling the promised Switch 2 patch for The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Remastered, addressing a number of issues in the game. Read more
item.description:
CD Projekt Red is currently rolling the promised Switch 2 patch for The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Remastered, addressing a number of issues in the game.
The headline changes are adjustments to image sharpening and resolution to "improve visual clarity and fidelity" - changes that have resulted from players saying the game looked blurry to them, particularly when played in handheld mode.
There are also, as we've seen in patches for other console versions of the game, changes to lighting in the game to reduce some of the brightness caused by the Remastered edition - one of the main areas of contention since its late September release.
The full list of changes in patch 5.01 for The Witcher 3 Remastered are as follows.
The Witcher 3 Remastered update overhauls the 11-year-old role-playing game, visually modernising it as well as adding new animations and tweaking some gameplay systems, including skills and enemy behaviour. It prepares the way for the new Witcher 3 expansion Songs of the Past, due to arrive next year, and is an extraordinarily generous upgrade in its own right.

item.description:
Next year's Call of Duty game will not be part of any of the franchise's existing sub-series. In an interview with The Game Business, Activision confirmed it's finally ready to create a new sub-series.
"We've already kind of stated that a future title is going to be a new sub-franchise and we've already kind of laid the groundwork there," Activision chief marketing officer Tyler Bahl said.
This year's game, Modern Warfare 4, is the final chapter in one of Call of Duty's most popular sub-franchises, which followed on from 2025's Black Ops 7, the 7th entry in the other popular Call of Duty sub-series.
Activision announced last year it's no longer going to release two back-to-back games form the Modern Warfare or Black Ops sub-series, and this presumably goes for future sub-series that get created. Bahl admitted that releasing back-to-back games in the same sub-franchise was something the community rejected.
"Yeah, I think we were pretty public about the idea of us going back-to-back with Modern Warfare 2 to Modern Warfare 3 and Black Ops 6 to Black Ops 7 was not something that our community was looking for," Bahl said.
"And even though there were different time settings and different ways to play the game[s] and lots of new features, that tonal shift is something that they were looking for us to [do]."
The most recent Call of Duty game in a new sub-franchise was 2021's Vanguard, which performed poorly and failed to establish a new sub-franchise within the larger brand. Incidentally, Vanguard was developed by Sledgehammer Games, which is understood to be the maker of next year's game - itself also a new sub-franchise.
2027's Call of Duty is rumoured to be set in the late 90s and early 2000s featuring a new setting with a new cast of characters. It's going to be critical to see how well the new sub-series sets itself apart from the existing duo, and whether it ends up getting a sequel.

item.title: Norwegian developer Funcom, creator of Dune: Awakening and Conan Exiles - and many other games - is entering a period of restructuring and bracing for layoffs as a result. You may remember the company making a similar move this time last year, months after the initial PC release of Dune: Awakening. Read more
item.description:
Norwegian developer Funcom, creator of Dune: Awakening and Conan Exiles - and many other games - is entering a period of restructuring and bracing for layoffs as a result. You may remember the company making a similar move this time last year, months after the initial PC release of Dune: Awakening.
Funcom is also appointing a new CEO, as long-time leader Rui Casais leaves the company after 22 years - with 11 as its leader - and Scott Junior steps into the role, having been at the company for 25 years and steered Dune: Awakening to market as executive producer.
The need to restructure follows the end of major development work on Dune: Awakening. Now that the console versions have been released - they arrived 22nd September with a new single-player mode - Funcom moves into live service operation mode, which seems not to require a development team as large.
"Dune: Awakening has been the biggest project we have ever undertaken, requiring many years of significant development resources across our studios," said Rui Casais in a press release. "Moving from full production into long-term post-launch development and operations requires a different organisation.
"While we would have wanted everyone who helped build Dune: Awakening to continue with us, we cannot sustain the size and structure required during peak development as we move into this next phase. My focus now is ensuring the process is as supportive as possible for everyone affected, and to treat our colleagues with the respect and transparency they deserve."
The press release noted that this will mean "a period of restructuring" for Funcom, and "reducing the size of the organisation", which yes, means "saying goodbye to valued colleagues". That process begins "now". Our thoughts are with the people affected.
As to Dune: Awakening and Conan Exiles' futures, Funcom said it remains "committed" to "supporting, expanding, and growing these games and their communities for years to come". The company pointed to the recent release of Conan Exiles' Enhanced edition and said it would continue to expand upon that.
Dune: Awakening initially launched last June on PC, billed then as an ambitious merging of survival game and massively multiplayer online role-playing game. The gist is that you're a desert-living person in the world of Dune, eking out a life for yourself on the sands, while avoiding the bloody massive sandworms that will eat you if you're not careful. Connor reviewed Dune: Awakening at the time and was really impressed.
Since its launch, however - which was big but numbers soon depleted - Funcom has set about making the game a more traditional survival game experience, enabling private servers and eventually, with the game on console, a single-player mode where you don't have to interact with other people at all. Funcom announced recently that 1 million "new survivors" had made the game their home, but that doesn't necessarily equate to sales as it's a Game Pass game as well.

item.title: Steam Next Fest 2026 starts today, offering PC players a chance to get their hands on a staggering number of playable demos. With the full count coming to more than double last year's event, concerns about generative AI 'slop', plagiarism, and discoverability are circulating Read more
item.description:
Steam Next Fest 2026 starts today, offering PC players a chance to get their hands on a staggering number of playable demos. With the full count coming to more than double last year's event, concerns about generative AI 'slop', plagiarism, and discoverability are circulating
The Steam Next Fest 2026 press page breaks down the full scope of this digital deluge of demos, with the full count currently sitting at 8,202. On the surface, this looks to be a great opportunity for people to discover a cool new game before the GTA 6-dominated month of November hits.
However, the everpresent shadow of generative AI continues to loom over the storefront. Last June, roughly 17 percent of the Steam Fest demos disclosed the use of generative AI, a substantial figure that may be larger due to the possibility of undisclosed gen AI use. The popularity of this software has not waned in the past 12 months either; if anything it's become more prevalent.
The issue of generative AI in games on Steam has evolved somewhat, too. The software has been used to clone games, and a troubling trend of up-and-coming indie games being copied and oozed onto Steam is a factor smaller developers have to contend with now. Alliance Arts suddenly cancelled the release of their upcoming spooky horror game Drunken Goddess Reflux Steam Fest demo because of this.
In a statement announcing the move, the developers of Drunken Goddess Reflux expressed concerns that the demo would be: "used to quickly imitate or replicate the game's presentation and gameplay with AI or other tools, and that such works could be released before our launch." These fears have merit. Another hot indie game - Needle in a Haystack - is now suffering a flood of quickly made copies.
There's also another consequence of this influx of games: discoverability. An indie developer making a demo in hopes of enticing people to their upcoming project has to fend off a mountain of other demos attempting the same thing.
It's a tricky problem, and a consequence of the propagation of generative AI tools. Whether these Steam Next Fest events - which have been excellent occasions to discover new games - will remain as useful an event for developers and gaming enthusiasts alike remains to be seen.

item.title: It may be hard to believe, given all the Call of Duty: Modern 4 pre-launch community drama and the beta's lower-than-expected numbers on PC, but the final game may have turned things around - so far, at least. Read more
item.description:
It may be hard to believe, given all the Call of Duty: Modern 4 pre-launch community drama and the beta's lower-than-expected numbers on PC, but the final game may have turned things around - so far, at least.
On Steam, Infinity Ward's final chapter in the Modern Warfare sub-series currently has a Very Positive (92 percent) rating based on over 3,100 user reviews. Modern Warfare 4's campaign early access went live Friday, and the review rating has been improving steadily as players have experienced more of the campaign's missions. Many have likely finished it by now; the campaign is a little over six-hours in length, after all.
Gaining access to the campaign on Friday required pre-ordering any of the game's editions digitally. Modern Warfare 4's official release isn't until 23rd October, which makes it hard to determine the current number of players, because SteamDB, our source for this data, can't reveal numbers without its tracking bot having a copy of the game.
Setting aside player numbers, the sentiment around Modern Warfare 4 is considerably more positive at the outset compared to last year's Black Ops 7, currently sitting at Mostly Negative (37 percent). While review ratings change over time with each major update, Modern Warfare 4 is currently the highest-rated Call of Duty in over a decade.
However, it's worth bearing in mind that the people playing the game are likely the series' most keen players, so perhaps they're more lenient towards it. We haven't had a chance to review the game yet, having only received code late last week, but IGN published a COD: Modern Warfare 4 campaign review on Friday, scoring it 8/10.
In the rebooted Modern Warfare series, the 2019 Modern Warfare game comes closest in average player sentiment with a Mostly Positive rating (79 percent). 2022's Modern Warfare 2 is far lower with a Mixed rating (45 percent). Outside of Infinity Ward's output, Black Ops: Cold War is close at Mostly Positive (79 percent).
Modern Warfare 4's next big moment is the anticipated release of DMZ, the game's extraction shooter mode. Like the campaign, DMZ is available early for pre-orders, unlocking tomorrow, 20th October. Finally, on 23rd October, traditional multiplayer becomes available, which is when we're likely to see a shift in user sentiment, if one is going to happen.

item.title: Battlefield Studios has responded after fans accused it of using AI to generate cosmetics after spotting a "Secuty" typo on a Battlefield 6 Season 5 skin. Read more
item.description:
Battlefield Studios has responded after fans accused it of using AI to generate cosmetics after spotting a "Secuty" typo on a Battlefield 6 Season 5 skin.
The studio acknowledged "candid feedback" from players in a statement on social media, insisting it had "hear[d] your concerns".
And though the statement did not mention AI - either to admit or deny using the generative tech - BattlefieldComm said that while the 'Secuty' typo will be addressed by a "correction update", an outfit with five pistols is intentional.
"First, let's dive into the 'Secuty' typo patches on the McNeil character," the studio wrote. "A correction update has already been planned for the Season 5 Phase 2 release. However, we recognise that letting a known visual error go live without quick acknowledgement creates confusion and erodes trust. We are reviewing how we communicate known visual bugs so you aren’t left wondering whether something was intentional or overlooked."
The five-pistol-touting Midnight Mirage skin, however, is described as an "intentional creative concept" and "a nod to over-the-top action movie tropes where an operative inexplicably has another backup weapon strapped to every spare inch of gear".
"That said, we understand how this could look unintentional when released alongside other cosmetic anomalies," the team added, and, specifically addressing the typo, said: "We take pride in the craft of our world and our gear, and seeing visual oddities slip through is frustrating for everyone."
Cosmetic Quality & Recent FeedbackOver the past week, we’ve seen conversation, memes, and candid feedback around a few of our latest skins and cosmetic items—specifically the standard issue McNeil skin with “SECUTY” typo.You called it out clearly, and we hear your concerns.…
The message did not say how the typo happened or address fan accusations that generative AI was used.
Season 5 launched in Battlefield 6 this week as planned, and though most of the new additions - new maps, weapons and vehicles, and gameplay changes - were well received, the season began on a low note due to those aforementioned accusations of generative AI use and a major hit to XP gain.

item.title: The PS6's memory and storage reportedly cost more than $680 between them. Read more
item.description:
The PS6's memory and storage reportedly cost more than $680 between them.
That's according to leaker Kepler_L2, who wrote that "RAM + NAND alone is over $680" in a NeoGAF thread in which Kepler_L2 was replying to a forum user who doubted an earlier cost estimate and suggested Sony could subsidise the PS6 to launch at $680.
In June, insider Kepler_L2 - who has previously made claims about hardware that have turned out to be true - claimed the console's bill of materials had climbed to close to $1,000, up from their earlier estimate of around $760.
It follows Sony Interactive Entertainment boss Hideaki Nishino telling investors in June that "as a principle, we do not intend to sell hardware at significant losses".
Kepler_L2 didn't say how they arrived at the figure, and Sony has not, of course, confirmed any PS6 specs or pricing.
We already know that console manufacturing is being heavily impacted by the ongoing component shortage, driven by the proliferation of AI datacenters, the war in Iran, and accusations of price fixing.
It's therefore possible that we'll have to wait a while for Sony's next console - a console that is very likely to ship without support for discs and go all-in on Sony's controversial 'all-digital future'.
Despite plenty of consumer outcry, the company has remained bullish in its commitment to scrapping discs by 2028 (the earliest, at this point, we're realistically going to see the PS6 on the market). It's also likely that Sony is going to push harder into subscriptions and cross-generational games.

item.title: UPDATE 19TH OCTOBER: Liquid Swords founder and CCO Christofer Sundberg has confirmed the studio's closure. Read more
item.description:
UPDATE 19TH OCTOBER: Liquid Swords founder and CCO Christofer Sundberg has confirmed the studio's closure.
Writing on LinkedIn, Sundberg said the studio was in discussions with "all parties involved in Liquid Swords" about continuing support for Samson, and though there's nothing yet to announce, "it's something we're working to resolve".
Sundberg also revealed that he's got plans to start a new studio "built with the current market in mind", and that he'll have more to share soon.
His full statement is as follows:
"Liquid Swords is closing its doors. I've done everything I can to make this succeed, and I'm very proud of what we achieved together.
"It's been a hell of a ride and a lot of fun, even when the circumstances gave us very little to laugh about. Building a studio, creating Samson and releasing it on PC and consoles took an enormous amount of work from people who cared deeply about what we were making.
"The console versions met with much greater success than the PC release. We got them out, but that success wasn't enough to get the company across the finish line. Market conditions and some bad business decisions brought us here, and I own my part in that. I can look honestly at what went wrong and still be proud of what we built.
"We're also in discussions with all parties involved in Liquid Swords about how we can continue to support Samson the way the game deserves. There's nothing to announce on that yet, but it's something we're working to resolve.
"To everyone who worked at Liquid Swords, our partners and everyone who supported us and played Samson: thank you. You gave us plenty of reasons to keep fighting, and the work we did together deserves to be remembered for more than how the company ended.
"We make mistakes, we learn, we fall, we rise up, we move on. That's sometimes a painful process, especially when it affects people you care about, but I refuse to give up. I never give up.
"I'll be back at it again soon and will share more about my plans for a new studio. It will be built with the current market in mind, with a solid foundation and business decisions that give the games and the people making them room to succeed. The lessons from Liquid Swords will be part of how I build it.I still love making games.
"There's a lot more I want to do, and I intend to get on with it."
ORIGINAL STORY 18TH OCTOBER: Swedish studio Liquid Swords, maker of action game Samson, has reportedly been put into bankruptcy.
Break It (thanks, PC Gamer) reports that the studio's almost 30 employees will be compensated by the state, and that the bankruptcy trustee is looking for a buyer.
The original report suggests Liquid Swords has not paid its developers for months, but the bankruptcy order, thought to have been issued on 12th October, should mean unpaid salaries will be covered by Sweden's state wage guarantee.
Christofer Sundberg, who co-founded Just Cause developer Avalanche Studios, set up Liquid Swords in 2020.
Samson: A Tyndalston Story, the studio's first game, launched on PC on 8th April, followed by PS5 and Xbox Series X/S on 21st September. The studio initially had difficulty securing a publisher, and reviews were ultimately mixed with players complaining of technical and performance issues.
Liquid Swords is the latest studio hit by job losses. On 22nd September, Xbox confirmed 268 more layoffs and moved Rare and World's Edge under Activision, which will now develop the next Halo game, while Supermassive Games appears to have lost more than 70 staff earlier this month.
Xbox also said that day it was beginning consultation on a proposed closure of Ninja Theory after two separate agreements for the studio fell through.

item.title: God of War Laufey's Collector Box will cost £129.99 and will not include the game. Read more
item.description:
God of War Laufey's Collector Box will cost £129.99 and will not include the game.
That's according to an update on the PlayStation Blog, which confirms the box, priced at $149.99 and €149.99, contains a light-up Faye statue, a 51-card Oracle Deck, and a mini artbook.
The eight-inch statue shows Faye, Phranque, and Rue taking on Begtse's soldiers, and "Phranque will light up when the statue is plugged into a USB power source" (thanks, ScreenRant).
The Oracle Deck has custom illustrations by Megan Lara on every card, and Sony describes it as "a beautiful representation of your adventure through the Everywhen". The mini artbook collects concept art of the game's characters, creatures, and environments, "hand-selected by our talented art team at Santa Monica Studio".
The box will be available in "highly limited quantities exclusively direct from PlayStation (where available)" on 16th February 2027, the same day God of War Laufey launches on PlayStation 5.
Pre-orders are now open "while supplies last".
This isn't the first collector's box to skip the game. Rockstar's £349.99 GTA 6 Collector's Box, due on 19th November, is merch only, for example, and Bungie has previously sold Destiny 2 collector's editions without the expansion code.
Last month, The Last of Us director Bruce Straley apologised to the God of War Laufey team at Sony Santa Monica for saying he was "not excited" about the upcoming game's gameplay.

item.title: "Let me be honest from the start: nobody was waiting for this. The world has many needs, and a Game Boy cartridge with no game inside it was not high on the list." So begins Dr Marcel Pflug's explanation for one of the most unexpected projects I've come across in a while: a Game Boy reference museum that isn't just a Game Boy reference museum; it's one that works on a Game Boy cartridge. Read more
item.description:
"Let me be honest from the start: nobody was waiting for this. The world has many needs, and a Game Boy cartridge with no game inside it was not high on the list." So begins Dr Marcel Pflug's explanation for one of the most unexpected projects I've come across in a while: a Game Boy reference museum that isn't just a Game Boy reference museum; it's one that works on a Game Boy cartridge.
"I run this museum, a project that catalogues everything around the little grey machine," Pflug writes on the Game Boy Museum website, "and one day a thought took hold that I could not shake, mostly because it made me laugh. Every object in the collection is a museum piece, so what if the museum itself became one of them? A cartridge that plays nothing, that you slot into a real Game Boy, and that turns the machine into a guide to its own world. An exhibit about the collection, living inside the collection."
The Game Boy Museum, in its original website form, features a museum's worth of knowledge and exhibitions focusing on Nintendo's classic handheld. There's a dizzying array of Game Boy product shots, all neatly presented and organised; there's an entire archive of peripherals, including things as incidental as cables; there's a guide charting every micro-adjustment to the Game Boy's hardware over the ages; and there's a journal area collating hundreds of articles about the handheld. There is, in other words, a lot.
As comprehensive as it is, though, presenting it all online to browse using modern computers and devices is relatively straightforward. But cramming that onto a cartridge for a device made in 1989 is an entirely different matter. So there were immediate obstacles for Pflug's project. The Game Boy, Pflug discovered, is "a spectacularly bad e-reader", due to the limited 255 "blocks" it can show on screen. That's not a lot when you consider several blocks are used for every letter of text, and the museum is primarily a text-based affair. "Reading a museum on a Game Boy, it turns out, is a game of inches," Pflug notes.
He also wanted the Museum to display QR codes, as a way to point people towards photographs he couldn't show on the Game Boy, feeling there'd be something "quietly wonderful" about getting a piece of tech from the 80s to talk to a phone from the 2020s. But, of course, QR codes were never meant to be displayed on a Game Boy. As Pflug explains, they were created in 1994, well after the handheld's release, "to track parts on a Japanese car-factory floor". It was Toyota's factory, if you're wondering (that's your quiz bonus point).
Similar bespoke solutions were needed for things like displaying an image of Pflug in the credits, because apparently you can't simply convert a photo into the tones of a Game Boy screen. "The face becomes one pale blob, the eyes turn into two black holes, and you have accidentally drawn a skull," says Pflug, which sounds rather appealing to me. He also ended up drawing the cartridge's title screen by hand, pixel by pixel, which took a lot of work - so much that he quickly abandoned plans to include an entire museum hall with display cases. And on some days, nothing he tried worked at all. "That is rather the point of building on hardware this old," he notes. "It makes you earn every screen."
"It is a homage to the machine," Pflug elaborates in his write-up, "and a small attempt to keep this knowledge where it came from in the first place, on the Game Boy itself, so that whatever happens to websites and servers and me, the little grey brick can still tell you its own story." That feels like a particularly relevant sentiment in 2026, when the world is on the cusp of an AI makeover, or perhaps takeover, and when projects such as these are theoretically achievable in minutes rather than years.
How long the project took to complete, Pflug isn't able to easily calculate, because it apparently "came together over many evenings and weekends across several years", with significant gaps in between. He builds things as a hobby when he has the time and the inclination: this isn't his day job, nor his only project. He has a fairly important-sounding corporate role and he also runs a free guitar portal called Sticky Tunes in his spare time. That's alongside a passion for being out in nature, and they all compete for his attention, so there's never quite enough time to go around.
"The truth is that programming and tinkering relax me," he says. "They let me forget the world for a while. And since - if we are honest - nobody has been waiting almost 40 years for the particular solutions I chase, there is something very freeing about it: I am doing it purely to satisfy my own curiosity and to challenge myself." And doing something for the sake of doing it, for the pleasure of doing it, feels like a fierce forehand return against the expediency of AI-generated results if ever I've heard it.
Pflug's Game Boy project feels proudly human in the face of AI, which I admire, and I tell him so when we speak. "For me, the Game Boy is not just a handheld," he offers by way of explanation, "it carries the feeling of a whole generation, the way a Walkman or a particular pair of trainers does for people who grew up then."
It's now been several months since Pflug's account of the Game Boy project first surfaced, and I was keen to hear how the world had responded to it since then. "The reaction surprised me," he reveals, "in the nicest way." He was especially warmed to see the project spread beyond the English-speaking parts of the world, all the way to the Game Boy's birthplace in Japan. "That it resonated at the source felt like a small gift," he says.
The Game Boy Museum cartridge project is essentially finished at this point, barring a few small twiddles, but the work doesn't ever entirely cease. Pflug plans to update the build "at least" once a year to keep it current with the Game Boy Museum's archive, "so the little cartridge grows as the game does". Nor is this the end of Pflug's Game Boy adventure; although the cartridge project has wound down, the lessons he learnt making it have led to something else - something equally unexpected. A second cartridge: the GB Test Lab.
"It does the opposite of a game," Pflug explains. "You slot it into a Game Boy and it examines the console itself. It can name the exact cartridge slot contact or memory bit that misbehaves; measure how worn the buttons are; test the printer and the link port. The idea is to give the people who collect, restore, and repair these machines something genuinely useful." People, in other words, like him.
Pflug says he's also learnt a lot about the Game Boy Printer while wrestling with QR codes, so he's working on another tool that turns it into a "a proper label printer". Why? Well, why do anything? To learn, to connect with other people doing the same, to honour something you like. To be human; to be curious.

item.title: A remaster of cult 2004 RPG Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines may be in the works. Read more
item.description:
A remaster of cult 2004 RPG Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines may be in the works.
In a post on the r/GamingLeaksAndRumours subreddit, a user wrote: "I can confirm that it is in the works. NOT a Remake, but a Remaster, with some caveats. That's all I can say".
The poster says they have "previously leaked info on multiple other games", including that Forza Horizon 6 is set in Japan, but of course, all we can do is treat this as an unsubstantiated rumour for now.
Their post follows an earlier thread about a possible Bloodlines remake, which they describe as having "kind of leaked" the news already.
Separately, another post on the subreddit, flagged "Grain of Salt", links to a thread about the band Genitorturers, which was involved with the original soundtrack, mentioning a Bloodlines remake.
No remaster has been announced.
ICYMI, Bloodlines 2 wrapped up development in June with its final post-launch update.
The leaker also describes a "dire situation" in the games industry, saying they "expect many games that are in development right now to not see the light of day".

item.title: Sega and Creative Assembly are temporarily removing Total War: Shogun 2 - Complete Edition from sale just days after release. Read more
item.description:
Sega and Creative Assembly are temporarily removing Total War: Shogun 2 - Complete Edition from sale just days after release.
In a statement shared on Twitter/X, the companies said they are aware the game "has fallen short of both your expectations and our own standards".
The companies are working "with platform holders to temporarily remove the game from sale and to reinstate the original game while we investigate the issues".
"Existing owners will still be able to access and play the game," the statement added.
Sega and Creative Assembly say they are also "working closely with our development partner to identify the causes of these problems, deliver improvements", with the aim that the Complete Edition meets "the quality standards players expect from Total War".
The Complete Edition launched on 13th October. The statement does not detail the issues or say when the game will return to sale.
The statement does not use the term AI at all, but many fans believe it's at the root of the "issues", pointing out "hokey upscaling" and what they believe to be evidence of AI in the Complete Edition.
Within days of release, Shogun 2 - Complete Edition's Steam score plummeted to "overwhelmingly negative" with just 15 percent of the game's more than 4,000 reviews leaving something positive. If you head to the game's Steam page now, you're warned that the game "is no longer available on the Steam store".
Last month, we reported that the CEO of Professor Layton developer Level-5 apologised after confirming that generative AI was used in the studio's recent showcase. Level-5 is not alone, of course - many other game companies, including Krafton, Square Enix, EA, and more, have invested heavily in AI tech.

item.title: Valve is beta testing Steam Achievement Sets, a feature that lets developers group a game's achievements into collections. Read more
item.description:
Valve is beta testing Steam Achievement Sets, a feature that lets developers group a game's achievements into collections.
In an announcement, the company said that games "live longer than ever, continuing to receive updates through new DLC, expansions, and seasons", but that achievements added with new content "can be hard to discover and can accidentally break the completion status of players who have already finished the game".
That's why developers can now specify the number of sets and the purpose of each "to match their game's specific needs", so one game might group its achievements into single-player and multiplayer groups, while another could use eight class-based sets. Players still unlock achievements as usual, and Steam then sorts what they've unlocked into the developer-created sets, which Valve says makes it "easier to see what you have completed and to find other related achievements you can unlock next".
Each set has its own progress bar, and completing one adds a "set complete" trophy to the player's profile. If new achievements are later added to a set, completion is "preserved".
Developers can also create new sets as a game grows, which Valve says makes it "easy for returning players to see what new things they can unlock, while also preserving their prior completion status until they play again".
There are two types of set. Base Game sets "contain achievements that can be earned by all players who play a game", with progress and trophies shown in blue, while DLC sets group achievements that can only be earned once additional content has been bought and are shown in purple.
Interestingly, DLC achievements "are not included in your overall game progress until you have access to the content", so players can track what they have unlocked in new content separately.
Developers can also archive individual achievements or entire sets, which Valve says could suit "season-based games or enabling time-limited holiday achievements". Players who had already unlocked an archived achievement or set "will still see it on their profile", but archived achievements "won't show up on the profile pages of users who missed the unlock nor block their progress toward completing a set or game".
Alongside the sets comes an updated achievements page, reachable from the Games List on the web and from games in the Steam Library, and Search now has filters for specific sets and for locked or unlocked achievements. Players can also compare their progress with "up to three friends, including rare achievements, completed sets, and progress in DLC sets".
Elsewhere, the Perfect Games tab is now called Completed and "expands to show both completed games and games with completed achievement sets", games played via Family Sharing now appear in the Games List, and friends who played a game that way are eligible for friend comparison. Store and Library pages will also show if a game has achievement sets.
The beta is available to players and developers, and Valve says it will "continue making improvements during the beta", adding that "as developers begin using the new tools, you'll start seeing these changes appear for supported games".
Games that have already added achievement sets are Against the Storm, Age of Wonders 4, American Truck Simulator, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, Crusader Kings 3, Dredge, Euro Truck Simulator 2, Forza Horizon 5, Flock Around, He is Coming, LEGO Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight, Left 4 Dead 2, Portal 2, PowerWash Simulator, PowerWash Simulator 2, Team Fortress 2, and Victoria 3.
Valve's PC digital store and social platform set a new user concurrent record last Sunday, clocking up a staggering 43,505,724 users. Meanwhile, Epic Games isn't lifting its foot off the gen-AI pedal, having vibe-coded a new Epic Games Launcher in an attempt to outrun Steam, by far the most popular digital games marketplace on PC.

item.title: Footage of a reportedly cancelled Assassin's Creed game set in ancient China has emerged online, including stealth kills, the series' leap of faith, and a spinning umbrella weapon. Read more
item.description:
Footage of a reportedly cancelled Assassin's Creed game set in ancient China has emerged online, including stealth kills, the series' leap of faith, and a spinning umbrella weapon.
Called Assassin's Creed Destiny, it was reportedly being made for current platforms at Tencent-owned TiMi Studio Group, which also worked on mobile game Assassin's Creed Jade.
According to MP1st, the clips were taken from portfolios belonging to people who worked on it, and most come from a prototype built in February 2025. It's thought Destiny's setting was 206 BCE, nine years after Jade's 215 BCE.
The main mission has a female assassin heading into a sacred palace under siege from the army of the warlord Xiang Yu, in search of a mysterious artefact, and an early-stage boss encounter involving the warlord also appears.
Elsewhere, a male character uses parkour to dispatch enemies, while a temporary test area shows the player using an umbrella-style spinning weapon, with ink-brush ability icons and a health bar on screen.
Codename Jade got a namecheck back in March alongside "several other projects currently in the works, all at different stages of development". There was talk of "bringing co-op back to Assassin's Creed", and a vague nod to a cancelled game, but we're still no closer to a release date for Jade or indeed any other firm details about the mobile game.
The bad news continued this week, too, when Ubisoft proposed closing Finnish studio RedLynx, creator of the Trials series of games, and announced significant layoffs at Assassin's Creed: Black Flag Resynced studio, Ubisoft Singapore.
"Today, we informed our teams of a proposal to close RedLynx in Finland, subject to the local change negotiation process, which would affect up to 52 positions," Ubisoft said in a statement seen by Eurogamer. "At Ubisoft Singapore, 70 positions have been impacted to align the studio with upcoming production needs. The studio remains an important part of Ubisoft's global production organisation."

The update will also, quite rightly, let you pet dogs and cats.
The team is also addressing some technical issues, including an update to the FrameGen technology and dedicated settings.
Here’s what’s coming to The Blood of Dawnwalker with Update 1.1 planned for next week: pic.twitter.com/yi5yaoh3Us
And over 1,100 other improvements and fixes.
The patch is expected to roll out next week.

Bertie praised its novel time-limiting structure and freeform approach, as well as its enjoyable quests and characters, writing: "CD Projekt Red alumni create a familiar dark fantasy adventure, but one with bold and provocative ideas of its own, that's mostly, enormously successful".

item.description:
I'd nearly forgotten Over the Hill's predecessor, Art of Rally, was a racing game. But that's not meant as a slight. It's just that, for all the happy hours I poured into it, I don't recall doing a single race. Instead, it was the aimless meandering, the soothing rhythms of exploration and absent-minded collectible hunting in its free-roam mode that held me transfixed. So the fact Over the Hill completely jettisons the racing stuff and leans entirely into the meditative bit - it even starts with a golden Buddha statue running you through the basics, which probably tells you everything you need to know - is exactly my kind of thing.
Over the Hill very much feels like Art of Rally's free-roam mode writ large. Here the entire focus is on unhurried off-road exploration across large open swathes of stylised, vividly hued wilderness. And the vibe of its minimalist roaming, its uninsistent structure, very definitely skews toward 'chill'. Which is to say, if you're the kind of person who craves direction and explicit goals, or who's looking for speedy racing thrills, I don't think this is the adventure for you. But if, like me, you count yourself among the sandbox explorers, the curious meanderers, the tranquility seekers of the world, it offers its own special kind of driving thrill.
And it begins, of course, with some wheels; initially attached to a 4x4 "trail" vehicle whose handling is about as far removed from 'spritely' as you can go. As the Buddha bestows its off-road wisdom on you, you'll bounce awkwardly over rocks, crawl sluggishly up hills, and winch yourself through squelching mud in the most unbecoming fashion, switching between low and high gears for better traction depending on the invariably challenging terrain. Even a few hours in, with a few new vehicles and upgrades to your name, the pace remains a slow, careful one as you ride through the undulating woodland of the Canadian Valhallas or the boulder-strewn Algerian desert. It doesn't take long to learn caution is almost always the best approach, unless you enjoy extracting yourself from a forest with a 65-point-turn.
It's a game for patient souls, then, but if you can adapt to Over the Hill's unhurried (some might even say glacial) rhythms, it's a lovely world to be in - lilting guitars and gentle harmonicas providing a soothing accompaniment as you trundle ever onward toward your next vague, self-determined goal. Developer Funselektor shapes its game with the lightest of touches, filling its attractive open-world maps with enigmatic question marks - potential points of focus for your meandering - and unlockable camps that act as fast-travel points. Here, you can also speed up time if you want to escape the rain and whipping sandstorms, or if you fancy a hair-raising nighttime jaunt, or simply wish to watch the sun rise at dawn.
As for those question marks, sometimes they'll reveal nothing more than an abandoned crate containing a silly cosmetic when you reach them - a yeti-themed car antenna, perhaps, or a kayak you can stick on your roof for some wilderness flair (and to differentiate yourself from your pals if you fancy a knockabout roam in multiplayer). Other times you'll trigger a succession of curated trail route waypoints, tempting you across treacherous terrain - cautiously circling the rocks around a lake's perimeter, say, or winding along a perilously uneven precipice to reach a distant overhang - to secure your reward at the end. Sometimes, too, you'll find an abandoned truck you'll need to tow back to homebase, or maybe you'll simply stumble upon a lovely view.
But really, these are just excuses; lures to keep you moving and exploring the world. And actually, I kind of think it's more enjoyable to forget the map completely and just let your whims guide you across the tricksy terrain, adjusting your course should the telltale glow of a new mystery come into frame. Because it really is about the journey here. Every inch of Over the Hill's wilderness is its own kind of puzzle, each curve of the landscape threatening minor frustrations where little victories can be won, as you plot the most advantageous route in real-time; winding a gentle path across a river bank waiting to suck you into the mud, say, or across a blockade of boulders liable to get you wedged if you try to rush through.
Gradually you begin to realise Over the Hill isn't quite as formless, and its maps as disorderly, as they initially seem. You'll take a meandering path toward a tempting waypoint, only for it to remain tantalisingly out of reach unless you can puzzle a circuitous route through treacherous canyons and across the rickety bridge that offers final passage. And Over the Hill's minimalist progression builds on that further: some points of interest are properly inaccessible until you've got enough points - earned as you explore the map - to upgrade your vehicle. So ever onward through the untamed wilderness you go.
As you do, the sun rises and falls into starlight; rain batters the landscape before the clouds part again onto skies of blue. There's wildlife too - foxes, moose, owls, camels, bears, and more - so why not slow down and take some photos for your compendium? Why go fast at all in fact, Over the Hill seems to say, when you could relax, breathe, and simply take it all in?

item.title: Hello and welcome back to our regular feature where we write a little about the games we've been playing. This week, Connor plays a classic, and ticks it off his bucket list; Sherif isn't sure about a first-person shooter foray into Soulslikes; Matt visits a South Pacific island volcano and Jim Henson's Labyrinth, all in one game; and Bertie discovers that playing D&D with kids is enormously entertaining.
