item.description:
Hello and welcome back to our regular feature where we write a little about the games we've been playing. This week, Connor plays a classic, and ticks it off his bucket list; Sherif isn't sure about a first-person shooter foray into Soulslikes; Matt visits a South Pacific island volcano and Jim Henson's Labyrinth, all in one game; and Bertie discovers that playing D&D with kids is enormously entertaining.
But enough of that: what have you been playing this week?
And don't forget we have an entire dusty archive of previous What We've Been Playings, just in case you don't trust your memory and want to check which games you've played, and see what you thought of them.
I spent some time crossing a game off my bucket list. FTL has been sitting in my Steam library for years, untouched and unloved. When people have talked about FTL, I have smiled and nodded, knowing the game's merits and yet, to my shame, without any firsthand experience of it.
That ended this week! I booted up FTL and threw myself at it with gusto. The game is immediately engaging; I took great joy in figuring out intricate strategies that helped me to reach the final boss, even if I've yet to take it down (that drone phase is brutal).
I loved a moment when I learned that rather than manually having a crewmate extinguish fires, I could open the airlock doors and make a little path to the blaze. I felt properly smart when I figured it out. So yeah, here's to those bucket list classics! Next up for me is Dwarf Fortress.
I've been meaning to play the demo for Guns of Eschaton since its release and finally got to it this week, just in time for its 8th December release date announcement.
It's a first-person Soulslike, which is already a strange pairing, but one where - perhaps more surprisingly - melee combat is secondary. Your main weapon is a single-action revolver, though you later access other era-appropriate firearms. Eschaton is set in a supernatural, folk tales-inspired Wild West (Weird West?), one where magic, superstition and even faith are weaved into its fabric.I went in expecting very little; I simply didn't know if a first-person shooter could work as a Soulslike. And after about two hours with it, I'm still not sure I have a solid idea of the gameplay flow.
Due to the game's nature, most enemies will be at a distance, and it's very common for someone to shoot you from somewhere that you don't see. If you're even a little bit slow to hear that shot and parry the bullet, that's half of your health gone. A couple of encounters in the demo reminded me of some terrible tactical shooters: the slow peeking and hoping the AI doesn't one-shot you; the ammo scarcity that stops you taking any risks; the works.
It didn't help that the game's controls were mapped to controller buttons I didn't expect and couldn't change (B to jump, what?). Fighting with controls in a game as challenging as Eschaton isn't something I want to do. I felt so inadequate at playing the game that I went looking for other people's impressions to see if I'm alone in my feelings, but I am not.
I'm still going to keep Eschaton on my radar. The fantasy of a Soulslike gunslinger is just too specific to ignore. Maybe next time I'll play with a mouse and keyboard.
I had a lovely time when I shoved my head in Valve's new Steam Frame a few weeks back, and an equally lovely time playing far more Walkabout Mini Golf than I probably should have done, given all the other VR games I wanted to play. Well, the mini golf infatuation has not ended.
Walkabout Mini Golf is, if you don't already know, exactly what it sounds like: multiplayer mini golf, but in VR. The swingy ball-putting business feels great, entirely natural, thanks to those motion controls. But what really makes it work is developer Mighty Coconut's phenomenal, fantastical mini-golf course design. There's a little bit of everything across its main courses and dirt-cheap DLC: holes situated around 1950s-style Hollywood movie lots; courses inspired by Atlantis, Jules Verne, and Mount Olympus and its incumbent Greek Gods; matches winding precariously up and down red rock mesas, and even jaunts though Jim Henson's Labyrinth.
It's all good stuff; a wonderfully relaxing way to unwind solo or with a couple of helmet-owning chums. Sure, the air mightn't be as fresh in Steam Frame as it is outside, but my immediate outdoors doesn't include an easily accessible South Pacific Ocean island volcano, so there's that.
I also had a bash at Marvel Cosmic Invasion, at long last, this week. It's retro-styled, side-scrolling, co-op beat-'em-up starring all of your favourite Marvel heroes, probably. There's Captain America, there's Spider-Man, there's Storm, there's Wolverine. There's Cyclops, who's always struck me as a video game character first and foremost. It's good fun. There's a cool tag-team system whereby you can switch between two heroes, temporarily calling the other hero for help and special moves, and there are loads of over the top power-attacks. And you can fly. That sounds trivial but it feels enormously powerful just hanging in the air like that. A perfect couch co-op game.

item.title: Analogue - creator of various fancy retro-focused game consoles - has detailed its newly announced Mega Sg+ and Super Nt+: revised editions of its earlier Mega Sg and Super Nt machines, capable of playing original Sega and Nintendo cartridges with modern advancements. Read more
item.description:
Analogue - creator of various fancy retro-focused game consoles - has detailed its newly announced Mega Sg+ and Super Nt+: revised editions of its earlier Mega Sg and Super Nt machines, capable of playing original Sega and Nintendo cartridges with modern advancements.
Analogue's first stab at the Super Nt launched in 2018, while the Mega Sg arrived one year later. Both machines' imminent upgrades feature, as per the company's announcement, "an FPGA designed in-house from scratch and backed by more than a decade of development. Rock solid. No emulation. Purpose-built 1080p for 2D gaming. Zero lag. Total accuracy."
As for compatibility, the Mega SG+ is said to be 100 percent compatible "with the 2,180+ Sega Genesis, Mega Drive, Master System, Game Gear, Mycard Adapter, Mark III/SG1000 game cartridge library", while the Super Nt+ is compatible with over 2,200 Super Nintendo and Super Famicom games.
Both consoles sport a redesigned "industrial" look, and support wireless controllers via bluetooth and 2.4GHz connectivity. Additionally, users can hot-swap cartridges without having to power down the machines - they simply need to quit their current game and switch them out. Furthermore, it's possible to power the consoles on and off using a controller now - and the required USB-C power supply and cable are included in the box.
If your interest is piqued, you'll be able to pre-order them on the 19th October via the Analogue website, with consoles shipping this December. The Mega SG+ is available for $219.99 in three variants - Japan, EU, and US - while the $219.99 Super Nt+ comes in Classic, SF, and Black.

item.description:
You can smell it in the air can't you? The chill in your nostrils and the earthy whiff as leaves fall and the sun departs for another year. Yes, autumn is here, meaning we're teetering on the cavernous hole of near-nothingness as the entire games industry gives GTA 6 the widest berth imaginable. But that doesn't mean there isn't stuff to be excited about, of course. And the latest edition of the Galaxies Showcase has chucked a few more things onto the 'ooooh intriguing!' pile. Actually, quite a lot of things given its nearly two-hour runtime; but while you can watch the full thing in its entirety if you've got the time, we've also picked out a few of the announcements that especially caught our eyes and highlighted them below. Was all this really just an excuse for Connor to enthuse about penguins? Perhaps!
I've been very excited about Bristol developer Friday Sundae's There are no Ghosts at the Grand ever since I saw it at a preview last year. It's one of those things that reads like a checklist of my very specific gaming interests, being part musical, part home renovation sim, and part ghostbusting mystery adventure, all unfolding in a dilapidated hotel in a British seaside town.
The idea is you've got 30 days to renovate it (exactly why is part of the mystery given its protagonist has motives so secret, he'll even try hiding them from the player), but there's plenty more to do besides: you can explore the cobblestone streets, go sailing out at sea, or take a scooter into the countryside as you attempt to uncover the truth about the hotel's strange past. By night, there are ghosts to deal with - and throughout all this, the cast is prone to bursting into song. And if that tickles your fancy in the same way it's tickling mine, you can play a Steam demo right now ahead of its December arrival.
AfterZero: The Last Drive is possibly the first Pacific Drive-like, in that it's a game about driving a car across a post-apocalyptic wasteland - where you'll scavenge, fix up, and upgrade your car, and build out your hideout. It's the work of 3DClouds, the studio mostly known for Formula Legends, but The Last Drive is an altogether different beast. There's a focus on environmental and traversal challenges, similar to the Snow/MudRunner games, or Over the Hill more recently. Its setting caught my eye, too, unfolding in a post-industrial world where it's always winter. Everything is covered in snow, and the reveal trailer hints there's a mystery at the heart of it all. Like Formula Legends, The Last Drive has a sort of blocky, inky artstyle that elevates its plastic toy-looking cars and objects, and it's releasing sometime in 2027 for PC (Steam), PS5, and Xbox Series X/S.
Contact Protocol is an eerie, grim-looking (in a good way) starship job sim that places you in the shoes of a security officer working for a greedy corporation. Your decisions, while surely horrid, are keeping a crew of miners alive as you set course for Jupiter's biggest moon. Aside from a killer premise, Contact Protocol has a wonderful aesthetic, offering a dirty, grisly look - full of delicious retro hardware - at a ruthless life among the stars. There's a demo available on Steam now, and the full game's out next year.
It's hard to explain why, but Late Shift immediately reminded me of Susanna Clarke's wonderful story Piranesi. I think it's to do with the game being about escaping from a world you find yourself trapped in. Maybe it's also just because there's a section with a white hallway.
On closer inspection, Late Shift, from developer AstroCat Studios, is probably more like Remedy's work, presenting players with a bizarre, incoherent world that they have to find their way out of. Specifically, it's a "short found-footage anomaly horror game", according to the Late Shift Steam page, told through the eyes of a missing cinema employee. Did you know former Eurogamer people Tom Phillips and Martin Robinson both used to work at cinemas? Perhaps it's their story Late Shift brings to life. The trailer announced the release of a Late Shift demo, and the full game is "coming soon".
Call me superficial, but I was onboard with Deperson the second I saw its artstyle. Developer Error Thing describes its game as a "self-reflective psychological horror adventure", and that begins when protagonist Aaron mysteriously finds himself in Indrija, a "nation consumed by surveillance and fear". I'm not entirely sure what genre we're dabbling with here on the gameplay front, but it's got an air of point-and-click puzzler to it and it sounds like there might be a bit of action too. "Sometimes you'll need to run. Sometimes you'll need to think carefully," says Error Thing. "Deperson is not a forgiving game." Whatever it is, though, it's certainly a looker, with a wonderfully unnerving hand-drawn animation style that's as surreal as it is striking. Deperson is set to launch sometime next year, but there's a demo out now on Steam, so I guess I know what I'm doing this weekend.
I had no idea about When Sirens Fall Silent until last night, but it stood out like a fart in a church during the Galaxies Showcase. This heavy psychological serial killer horror is the new game from Martha is Dead and Town of Light studio LKA, and I'm in love with the mood and styling of it. That's an odd thing to say given the subject matter, but its story appears to be told through a mixture of news reports, recorded interviews, and various pieces of media, all painstakingly styled with a mid-90s aesthetic. The result is something not unlike a true crime documentary, and I'm very fond of those.
The part I'm worried about, after seeing a pretty young woman in a plunging neckline top manacled to a chair in the opening, is that there's a questionably seedy undertone to the trailer. But reading more about When Sirens Fall Silent reveals it to be a story directly dealing with misogyny, trafficking, trauma, and - much more hopefully - redemption. It's got me fascinated, and it's due next year.
Now, in itself, a Knight Rider crossover trailer for Stuntman: Hollywood - a game already bulbous with Universal IP crossovers, ranging from Jurassic World and Miami Vice to Back to the Future - isn't especially exciting. But it has reminded me of my very tired, very confused time with it at this year's Gamescom. The gist is you, a stunt man, race around circuits as a bullish director bellows instructions at you in a bid to get the perfect shot.
That might be a daredevil hairpin bend on a freeway, or a race against a speedboat, or - in the case of the Jurassic World stage I played - an absolutely wild motorbike chase while a volcano erupts and dinosaurs pursue you. It's a game that demands pretty quick reactions, which is exactly what I didn't have as the show was drawing to a close and my Gamescom flu was setting in - and I was terrible. But I did enjoy the ridiculous spectacle of it all, and its Galaxies Showcase trailer has reminded me it's one to keep an eye on.
Kingdom is the game series that comes to mind when I see Wild n Chill. Because, just as Kingdom did fantasy town-building side-on and in pixel art, Wild n Chill is doing survival games in the same way. The vibes, as no one says, are immaculate: a person and their dog go out into the wilderness and set about chopping down trees and constructing a shelter and then building a solitary life out there. It's cosy, it's warming, it's peaceful.
I just wish you didn't have to be so crude as to chop down trees. It's a personal bugbear of mine, but you wouldn't presume to go out into the wilderness and start chopping down trees in real life, would you? You're overthinking it, Bertie. You're overthinking it. Wild n Chill is "coming soon" to PC (Steam) and now all of the consoles, by the looks of it. The brilliantly named Wombat Brawler is making it - a team that's made a few similar other games before.
Mr. Records immediately caught my eye when it showed up during Day of the Devs earlier this year. It's the latest game from Glee Cheese, the studio that made the enjoyable A Musical Story back in 2022, and tells the tale of a man named George who can travel through music. As he does, players are transported through vibrant worlds they'll need to rhythmically interact with. There seems to be a bit of a management focus too, given that each level, when completed, turns into a vinyl LP you'll need to match with customers back in your record store, and it all looks delightful. What's more, we now know it'll feature a level editor when it comes to PC in Q2 next year. Oh, and there's a Steam demo too.
One of the most surprising reveals at Galaxies was that Squad is coming to PS5 and Xbox Series X/S in 2027. Squad, if you don't know, is essentially a more approachable version of Arma, in that it's a realistic multiplayer shooter where class dependency and logistical planning are core elements of gameplay. Matches in Squad feature combined arms combat and take place across massive maps - up to 4x4km and supporting 100 players.
Squad on console, which doesn't yet have a release date, includes select maps from the PC version and it also supports console cross-play. But if you've ever seen gameplay of Squad, you'll know it seems nearly impossible to translate that depth - especially in UI and command options - to controllers, but the developers at Offworld Industries believe they've figured it out. They're so confident, in fact, there's an PS5 Alpha Preview available now until 25th October that anyone can play.
Listen, I don't need to sell you on the wonderful nature of penguins. Penguins are wicked; everyone loves penguins. A trailer showing a penguin waddling around and honking across town made for an outstanding sight last night. A penguin on a skateboard, pushing around a beachball, and swimming through storms and shipwrecks. Hell yeah, I'm down. My Penguin Friend - a "penguin puzzler" set on an unfamiliar tropical island, according to developer Good Gate Media - is coming to Steam next year, and can be wishlisted now.

item.title: Epic Games is officially working on bringing its battle royale shooter Fortnite to Linux. The announcement was tucked away at the bottom of Epic's widely mocked blog post revealing the new, "vibe-coded" Epic Games Store, which is also coming to Linux. Read more
item.description:
Epic Games is officially working on bringing its battle royale shooter Fortnite to Linux. The announcement was tucked away at the bottom of Epic's widely mocked blog post revealing the new, "vibe-coded" Epic Games Store, which is also coming to Linux.
At the time, Epic explained it's going to be working with Linux distro maintainers on a set of security requirements needed to run Fortnite. Distros - short for distributions - are operating system variants of Linux, each with its own goals and prioritised system operations. Valve's SteamOS, for instance, is based on Arch Linux. Because of the many discrepancies between Linux distros, each would need to implement Epic's security requirements individually if they want Fortnite to run on their operating system. Fortnite will arrive on Linux via the EGS launcher, but only if a "critical mass of distro maintainers" is reached. Epic didn't specify numbers.
This is big news for several reasons. For one, the move would likely make Fortnite playable on SteamOS PCs and handhelds, including Steam Machine and Steam Deck. Furthermore, even if that "critical mass" is never reached, Epic says its work will be available to other developers interested in bringing their games to Linux.
Perhaps the biggest reason this is a big deal, however, has to do with Easy Anti-Cheat, the Epic-owned anti-cheat service used in Fortnite and dozens of other games - including Dead by Daylight, Rocket League, Apex Legends, and even Elden Ring. While Easy Anti-Cheat does support Linux, including for some of the games just mentioned, many developers choose not to enable it, simply because its "Linux implementation couldn't offer the same level of protection as our Windows implementation," as Epic explained in a separate blog post. This is why many games that use Easy Anti-Cheat aren't playable on Steam Machine or Steam Deck. The post even names Valve specifically, saying the team will "continue its open line of communication" to support Steam hardware devices "to the maximum extent technically possible".
Part of the reason Linux has been a difficult problem for anti-cheat makers to solve is the platform's open nature, meaning certain - required - system-level protections are not guaranteed. On Windows, you can ask users to enable features like TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot, which create that secure environment once hardware requirements are met.
While some of that work can be done on Linux, it requires the interest and participation of distro maintainers. Easy Anti-Cheat plans to use Linux features such as signed kernel, signed kernel modules, and secure boot with attestation to achieve that goal. "These requirements build on work that distribution maintainers already do," explains Epic, "and the more distributions that meet these requirements by default, the fewer players will need to change their setup to play." The goal is to "bring the level of protection much closer to par with Windows".
There is no timeline for any of this at present, but Easy Anti-Cheat will test the announced plans in Fortnite first before making them available to other developers. In other words, if Fortnite gets a release date on Linux, you'll know the work has paid off and we're closer than ever to achieving anti-cheat parity between Windows and Linux.

item.title: The launch of a new live season is hard, and subtle changes to a game can have massive consequences when players get their hands on it. Wardogs proved this true with the launch of its second season this week, as players were able to unlock tanks on day one. Read more
item.description:
The launch of a new live season is hard, and subtle changes to a game can have massive consequences when players get their hands on it. Wardogs proved this true with the launch of its second season this week, as players were able to unlock tanks on day one.
The good news (or bad, depending on whether you feel you've missed out on a head start) is that this exploit has already been fixed. Players could drive just outside of their HQ, drop off pallets, and return to base to earn a sizable amount of XP. This, paired with faster XP gains for the Driver role allowed people to ascend rapidly through the Driver progression track and unlock tanks.
This was a problem, as unlocking anti-tank equipment via other progression paths took far longer than the measly few hours of dedicated grinding these Driver XP exploiters sat through, meaning the vast majority of players were unprepared to deal with the tanks - unless they made use of the exploit themselves and got their own.
In a post made to the Wardogs Discord, Bulkhead co-founder Howard Philpott said: "We're holding our hands up and we got a few things wrong". He went on to explain that a backend update was being pushed through that fixes a progression bug for the driver XP path, stomps out that aforementioned exploit, and also removes the Lonestar (blue team) cash and XP bonuses.
In a video released alongside the Discord, post technical designer Mark Tadros explained that players who were using the exploit "extremely" would be receiving 24 hour bans, though the number of players actually guilty of this falls below the 1,000 mark. Everyone else who partook in the practice, to a less absurd degree, appears to have been left alone.
It's the right call, and in all honestly a tragic result for what otherwise looked to be a direct, laser-targeted set of changes meant to take down some of Wardogs' trickier problems. In the first season, Driver XP was among the most time-consuming to get, so a change to improve that was a great idea. Likewise, the now-removed XP and cash bonus provided to the blue team was a smart solution to that faction, which struggled to win games back in season one.
Even so, the reaction in the community has been mixed. Some, understandably, are a little sad they missed out on the good XP gains. Others noted that this all happened while they were at work - the woe of the employed gaming enthusiast.
Nonetheless, Wardogs continues to prove its merit as a popular and enticing military FPS - and one of the breakout successes of the year. In our early access Wardogs review, we said the game's mix of competitive shooters' best bits with something entirely of its own made it "a brilliantly refreshing take on the genre".

item.title: CD Projekt Red has described its mysterious new game, which is currently known by its codename Hadar, as its "biggest project to date", revealing it's taken "several good years" to reach its current state, and it's still not even in pre-production. Read more
item.description:
CD Projekt Red has described its mysterious new game, which is currently known by its codename Hadar, as its "biggest project to date", revealing it's taken "several good years" to reach its current state, and it's still not even in pre-production.
That's according to CDPR joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski, who told Polish outlet PAP Biznes (translation by DeepL), "At this point we can say that we have a coherent vision of [Hadar's] world and its key elements. The team has started working on the game, although we're not quite at the pre-production stage yet. We're currently developing small prototypes, and we're also testing gameplay elements."
In the four years since its announcement, CDPR has said little about Hadar. However, we do know it won't be based on any existing property, unlike CD Projekt's other major titles - The Witcher having been created by Polish author Andrzej Sapkowski, and Cyberpunk 2077 by TTRPG maker Mike Pondsmith. (Incidentally, I've talked to both Sapkowski and Pondsmith about their work in this regard.)
Earlier this year, Nowakowski shared "an important development update" regarding Hadar's status. "Work on the project is progressing dynamically, and the team has established the foundations of this entirely new IP," Novakowski said in March. "Now, we have clearly defined distinguishing features of this world, and established key pillars that will not only provide the foundation for the game itself, but also, potentially, for other future products." He also mentioned that prototypes were being made in Unreal Engine.
We know from CDPR's most recent financial report in September that there were 33 people working on Hadar as of 31st July, so it's a small project compared to the studio's other titles. 519 people were working on The Witcher 4 at last count, 184 on Cyberpunk 2, and 84 on multiplayer Witcher game Project Sirius. However, Project Sirius was recently hit by layoffs.
Elsewhere in the interview, Nowakowski spoke more about The Witcher 4, which he called "our most ambitious project to date". He also said the studio wanted to "avoid repeating ourselves", so each game should "introduce new narrative and gameplay solutions" as well as "innovations" in main and side quests. "We want players to be confident that when they sit down to play this title, it pushes the boundaries of what an RPG can be and is technologically advanced," he said. The Witcher 4 was recently given a release target of 2028.
He also referenced the recent Remastered update for The Witcher 3, saying the company was "pleased" with sales, which "remain at a higher level than before the remaster", even now the launch discount period has ended. The Witcher 3 broke its Steam concurrent player records after the Remastered edition was released.
Finally, Nowakowski discussed the impact of Sony's decision to phase out PlayStation disc production starting 2028 - putting a possible Witcher 4 physical release in jeopardy. He reiterated much of what he's said before on the matter, saying that because console manufacturers make the discs, there isn't much CDPR can do if they decide to cease production. "A studio doesn't simply decide to release a game and then distribute the physical version itself," he said. "If a particular manufacturer completely shuts down the option to release games on physical media, they simply won't be available."

item.title: The latest game to pass a 1 million copies sold milestone is Control Resonant. Developer Remedy Entertainment broke the news yesterday, roughly three weeks after the game's release, revealing that Resonant is now the fastest-selling game in the Finnish studio's 31-year history. Read more
item.description:
The latest game to pass a 1 million copies sold milestone is Control Resonant. Developer Remedy Entertainment broke the news yesterday, roughly three weeks after the game's release, revealing that Resonant is now the fastest-selling game in the Finnish studio's 31-year history.
Remedy didn't share a digital/physical split, nor say which platform led sales, but these are good numbers for a Remedy game, and even more impressive considering the unusually packed September release schedule Resonant released into.
Remedy CEO Jean-Charles Gaudechon, who took over as boss of the company in February, called this a "very strong start". "Control Resonant is Remedy's first self-published release of this scale, launched into one of the most competitive windows in years alongside the industry's biggest names," Gaudechon said.
"We have always believed Control deserved an even bigger audience, and this launch shows what's possible: we see the game connecting with long-time fans while bringing a significant number of new players into the world of Control, which strengthens its long-term potential."
To that end, Gaudechon said Remedy would continue to build on its two "established" franchises in Control and Alan Wake, adding that: "Our focus is to build on what makes them special, support them, and grow them even further. There is a lot more to come from these worlds."
Although we don't have like-for-like sales data for the original Control, the game sold 2 million copies by the end of 2020, 15 months after launch. Alan Wake 2 - previously the fastest-selling Remedy game - by contrast took about two months to reach the 1 million milestone in 2023. Incidentally, Resonant is the lowest-rated of all three. Alexis Ong awarded it three stars in the Eurogamer review, saying it " feels like it's chasing the hallmarks of a live-service game while trying, only partly successfully, to echo the very deliberate structure and style of the genre storytelling that worked so well in the first game".
Control Resonant joins the likes of The Blood of Dawnwalker, Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Star Wars Zero Company, and Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve as recent releases that have all sold over 1 million copies.
If you're already playing Remedy's latest, or want to do so soon, the Eurogamer Control Resonant walkthrough is a helpful companion that'll make navigating the game's open world and making sense of its many character upgrades a breeze.

item.title: RuneScape: Reignited, a shiny new version of the long-running British MMORPG, has been cancelled less than two weeks after it was revealed. Read more
item.description:
RuneScape: Reignited, a shiny new version of the long-running British MMORPG, has been cancelled less than two weeks after it was revealed.
RuneScape Reignited - a major reveal during RuneFest earlier this month - was to be a game mode which would allow players to start fresh characters with a separate player-economy from regular RuneScape accounts, meaning they could only buy and sell items between themselves. Reignited accounts would also be prohibited from tackling bosses with regular RuneScape accounts. It was an attempt to court new players to the game. However, it was immediately met with fierce feedback from long-time RuneScape players.
Jagex announced the cancellation of RuneScape: Reignited in both a blog post and YouTube video, in which associate creative director Mod Ryan explained why the sudden U-turn had occurred: "We received a ton of different perspectives from all of you, and we truly appreciate everyone sharing their views.
"It is super important to us because the last time we didn't listen to player feedback, combat changed forever. And it has taken us over a decade to recover from that. Now I said on stage that we would not repeat the same mistakes of the past, and I truly stand by that. Considering this, we have made the decision to cancel Reignited."
The question on the mind of the RuneScape layperson is: why was the feedback so strong against Reignited? The core reasons come down to splitting the playerbase, and Reignited's potential to leave loyal players stranded.
Because of Reignited characters' totally separate player economies to pre-existing RuneScape accounts, and given their fresh-start nature, they would have been the obvious avenue for newcomers to the MMO. As such, the community would have been split in two, and non-Reignited accounts would have been starved of new blood that could keep it healthy and active in the months and years to come.
There was no option to transition an old RuneScape account to a Reignited one, either, so for veteran players who wanted to hop into this new exciting version of RuneScape, they'd have to throw away potentially years of progress and memories to do so, leaving their old accounts to wilt. We're talking thousands of hours and heaps of cash here.
However it's also worth noting Jagex did do this for a reason. The in-game economy of RuneScape has been hyper-inflated for a while now, making the process of creating a new character and progressing through to the endgame a daunting progress due to gargantuan prices. For example, a Bond (exchangeable for a month of premium membership) sells for 11.2m coins on Old School RuneScape. On regular RuneScape, a bond sells for 141.3m coins.
Reignited accounts would have - for all their faults - solved this problem, providing an easy on-ramp for those curious to check the game out. With Reignited's cancellation this problem still persists, leaving Jagex with the same hurdle it had in front of it a month ago, just with an extra bruise or two.
Thankfully for Jagex, RuneScape: Reignited was not the only reveal from RuneFest, and as Ryan went on to mention, RuneScape is getting an Adventure Guide update and other additions in December, and a free trial. In perhaps more exciting news, RuneScape 4, an entirely new MMO, was also revealed at the show.

item.title: Season 5 launched in Battlefield 6 this week as planned, and though most of the new additions - new maps, weapons and vehicles, and gameplay changes - were well received, the season began on a low note due to accusations of generative AI use and because of a major hit to XP gain. Read more
item.description:
Season 5 launched in Battlefield 6 this week as planned, and though most of the new additions - new maps, weapons and vehicles, and gameplay changes - were well received, the season began on a low note due to accusations of generative AI use and because of a major hit to XP gain.
Upon launch, Season 5 players discovered they weren't earning as much XP as they used to. To make matters more confusing, Battlefield Studios did not communicate any change to XP earn rates prior to the patch's release. The developer has now said the change was "unintended" and reverted XP earn-rates to their previous values.
"Following the launch of Season 5, backend configuration changes resulted in an unintended issue affecting XP earn rates across modes and hardware progression (such as weapons)," the official Battlefield Comms X account said. "These backend changes have now been reverted, and our team is actively monitoring telemetry to ensure earn rates return to intended levels across all experiences. Thank you for your patience and reports while we continue to track this."
Based on some testing, players could only earn a maximum of 300 XP per minute, which was well below the pre-patch rates. In the two days it took Battlefield Studios to respond, many assumed the amount of XP that could be earned had been quietly nerfed because the cuts coincided with the launch of Battlefield 6's Ultimate Shortcut Kit, which was made available to buy alongside Season 5's launch.
The Ultimate Shortcut Kit is a $30 / £25 purchase that fully levels up all classes (including gadgets and Training Paths) as well as 28 weapons and eight vehicles. In one click, you can unlock all of the weapons and vehicles' associated attachments and upgrades, not to mention skins and other level-gated customisation options. The Battlefield series has had similar shortcut packs in the past, but the proximity of this latest release to the unintended XP changes made players assume the worst.
It also didn't help that the season launched with a major returning exploit, and that some content caused suspicions of being created with generative AI, such as the Audacious Breach character skin. The arm patch of this skin spells 'Secuty' rather than 'Security".
Battlefield 6 has had issues with XP earn rates before - especially weapon XP. BF Studios spent months changing how XP and score were earned across the game, culminating in another boost at the start of Season 4.
But the game continues to run into unintended errors every so often in this regard. In June, BF Studios told players it changed XP Boosters to count down in-match, and not in real-world time. Players celebrated, only for the change to be reversed - and a similar thing happened again in the same month. A few weeks later, rival series Call of Duty announced that double XP tokens in Modern Warfare 4 and Warzone would only count down in matches, to much player celebration.

item.title: This generation's mega-game, Grand Theft Auto 6, will be eligible for The Game Awards 2026 by a matter of one day. Read more
item.description:
This generation's mega-game, Grand Theft Auto 6, will be eligible for The Game Awards 2026 by a matter of one day.
As highlighted on X by industry watcher Shinobi602, the cut-off date for this year's The Game Awards is 20th November, meaning GTA 6 - which arrives on 19th November - can be nominated across the show's various categories in 2026 and can potentially win. "Games must be made commercially available to customers on or before Friday, November 20, 2026, at 9pm PT," The Game Awards' website FAQ states.
The fit is so snug it might appear an exception has been made for Rockstar's game, but as Shinobi602 also noted, cut-off dates have been pretty similar each year, varying only by a day or two.
With GTA 6 in contention, the question becomes one of how much it could dominate proceedings. Rewind to Rockstar's last big release - Red Dead Redemption 2 in 2018 - and that game took home four awards: Best Narrative, Best Audio Design, Best Score/Music, and Best Performance (won by Roger Clark for his portrayal of protagonist Arthur Morgan).
The current TGA record holder - the game to beat - is Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, which last year took home nine wins, including the coveted Game of the Year award. Before Clair Obscur, the previous leader was Baldur's Gate 3, with six wins. GTA 6 is an order of magnitude larger in terms of budget, scope, and public anticipation than either game, especially Clair Obscur. The weight of expectation is on Rockstar, that's for sure.
The Game Awards 2026 takes place on 10th December, and usually bookends the year's industry activity, after which we all frantically try to decide what our personal games of the year are. Eurogamer, for full disclosure, is a member of The Game Awards jury, along with many other gaming websites.
Meanwhile, Rockstar released a new launch trailer for GTA 6 this afternoon, highlighting Jason and Lucia's steamy relationship - literally, as they frolic in the shower - and the strain of being in a high-stakes crime environment such as theirs.
Rockstar is also currently embroiled in an employment tribunal in Scotland revolving around the sudden firing of 31 staff from Rockstar North last year. Those affected call it union-busting, whereas Rockstar insists employees were fired for gross misconduct. The verdict is now not expected until well into November, almost bang on when GTA 6 releases.

item.title: Nintendo and Intelligent Systems have released an expansion pass for Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave, introducing a string of DLC additions to the tactical RPG starting today, and through into 2027. Read more
item.description:
Nintendo and Intelligent Systems have released an expansion pass for Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave, introducing a string of DLC additions to the tactical RPG starting today, and through into 2027.
The expansion pass, which can be bought on the Nintendo eShop for $34.99 / £29.99, comes in three parts. For those who buy it now, a selection of weapons are made available to use within the game. The second part of the expansion pass arrives this holiday season, and the final part arrives in 2027.
We already know a bit about what's coming in these latter DLC releases. The second portion features additional outfits for the game's cast, alongside three new allies: Aurora, Smyrnos, and Jurah.
The final segment of the pass looks to be the most substantial; introducing new stories to play, new allies, classes, and additional goodies. Those new stories make an already chunky game even larger, something that should give people a reason to go back to the RPG next year, and those yet to pick up the game, a convenient jumping-on point.
Fortune's Weave has been met with critical acclaim and sizable early sales figures. In Eurogamer's review, the game is described as "a synergy of everything that has made the series great for generations", and "a sumptuous feast of a game".

item.title: Rockstar Games has released the launch trailer for Grand Theft Auto 6 ahead of its 19th November release. Read more
item.description:
Rockstar Games has released the launch trailer for Grand Theft Auto 6 ahead of its 19th November release.
The trailer showcases the thrills set to come to the game on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S next month, with the footage itself apparently captured on the PlayStation 5. It features a selection of tidbits Grand Theft Auto fans may be interested in, including clips of heists in-action, one of which appearing to include a helicopter getaway gone awry.
There's also an intimate shower scene between the game's two protagonists, seemingly confirming the rumoured sex scenes and likely full nudity. There's a quick cut between a collection of other characters we'll run into, and various setpieces. Eagle-eyed viewers may spot some interesting details, including what appears to be an ankle tag on Lucia's leg, hinting she perhaps is out on parole. Jason also seems to get a reverse-charged phone call early on in the trailer, suggesting perhaps Lucia calling from jail.
The trailer opens with a shot of The Keys, a much-discussed portion of the GTA 6 that has been largely unexplored in prior trailers and gameplay footage. Also, the song playing in the background is a new standalone single from Justice called "Flower in a Hurricane", featuring Tame Impala, SZA, and the fantastic King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard.
The timing of the trailer is questionable, with Rockstar's employment tribunal ongoing in Glasgow, Scotland this week, and after a week of new leaked gameplay videos from the hacker Cyberleek.
As what is likely the final trailer for Grand Theft Auto 6 before it releases, it's certainly a good tone setter for those eager to hop in.

item.title: In my office, I have a collage of Ordnance Survey maps plastered across my wall. item.description:
In my office, I have a collage of Ordnance Survey maps plastered across my wall. They're from places I've lived - Derbyshire, East London, Bournemouth, Bristol - with cycle routes, country roads, and parks highlighted and circled. It's an atlas of my experiences, a living memoir of the places I've been and the things I've seen. There's magic in a map, its ability to remind you of the paths you've trodden and where you've yet to go.
Perhaps that's why I love Metroidvanias so much. Really, the game is the map. Is there anything more intoxicating than pushing your palms up against the walls supposedly keeping you in and knowing that - somewhere - there's a hidden path leading to the other side? Over the years, you develop an instinct for it; you get to play against the sadistic engineers of these labyrinthine spaces. 'I see your mysterious overhang,' you say, 'and jump through your roof. I see your egregious slab of a wall, and phase through its illusion.'
And Castlevania: Belmont's Curse has all this in spades. There are so many sly nuances tucked away around the streets of Paris and within Dracula's Castle that it's like I'm instantly transported back to my pre-pubescent self, nudging the D-Pad against every wall in Castlevania: Symphony of the Night in a belligerent attempt to sniff out its secrets.
Dead Cells developer Evil Empire's stewardship of the series honours the Belmont legacy with reverence. That begins with Rose Belmont, protégé daughter of Castlevania 3's main characters Trevor Belmont and Sypha Belnades, and a fearless vampire slayer herself. Belmont's Curse quickly sees her integrity tested and her resolve galvanised as Dracula's underlings wreck havoc in a ruined version of Paris in 1499. A lengthy tutorial introduces you to her central gimmick - a pack of tarot cards capable of sealing away the souls of those enthralled by the king of vampires - and then, before you know it, you're back in the bowels of Castle Dracula; jumping, and whipping, and navigating the sprawling map, more areas unlocking as you gain new skills. You sniff out clues as to what - and where - the main antagonists are, slowly revealed this interconnected web of intrigue as you become part of a story that's over 500 years old.
It's like 2D Castlevania never left. But in the 17 years since the release of Castlevania: The Adventure ReBirth (itself a remake of a 1989 game), there have been countless young genre upstarts vying for the 'Metroidvania' throne - Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown, Hollow Knight, Animal Well, Ori, and nu-Metroid all spring to mind. As Dracula languished in his perpetual undeath, the world has moved on. What he has spawned is now quicker, more aggressive, more mysterious. And Evil Empire understands that.
Some of what Belmont's Curse is laying down is absolutely inspired. The way that all the mirrors connect is sublime. A music-based puzzle in the depths of Notre-Dame cathedral is simply wonderful. The platforming gauntlet that takes you up the Clock Tower is great… when all the gears are working in tandem. But for all the sometimes genius design of its twisting corridors, its secrets-upon-secrets, and its sadistic environmental trickery, Belmont's Curse is too often undermined.
Maybe I've been spoiled by the litheness of Team Cherry's Hornet, or MercurySteam's driven version of Samus Aran. Because Rose feels awkward; an digital girl living in an analogue world. Her inputs, her attacks, her very being is defined by the classic eight directions of a D-pad, but everything else seems to exist on a more fluid plane. Some of Rose's abilities and attacks only work directly up, or down, or side-to-side. But all the enemies move in more organic ways, or throw their weapons in nice, flowing arcs. And it's the same for traversal. Trying to use her whip on enemies or anchors if you're not in some specific, awkward spot is a nightmare - and often turns smartly designed platforming segments into excruciating exercises in fighting with the game and its engine, instead of enjoying the puzzle. There's a constant, unpleasant tension between how I'm forced to move and how the world around me works.
Too often, Rose gets stuck between an enemy and its shield and stacks damage upon damage; your whip doesn't quite glue to where it's supposed to and you're sent back to the checkpoint, again. If I was being generous, I could argue it's a mechanical manifestation of Rose's curse; a plague of her legacy that holds back her true power as she wrestles with the consequences of legacy. But the awkward controls and framerate plummets - even on PS5 Pro - cause so many deaths, it's just irritating.
Furthermore, while I'm all for sadistic game design - I don't think I'd be playing a Metroidvania if I wasn't - there are times where Belmont's Curse feels mean-spirited, rather than playfully devious. Some of the checkpointing is unduly punishing, and the way in which you access fast travel and ease the pain of backtracking (something I'm reluctant to spoil) is needlessly convoluted and frustrating. Taking away the map in the most dizzying locale? I don't think that's as smart as the game thinks it is; it just makes for exasperating busywork.
Never is this tension between design and execution more egregious than in the boss fights. Some are really smart mechanical gauntlets that test your twitch reflexes and stamina; some are genuinely funny, simple encounters. Others are over-designed, trying to cram too many ideas in and ending up feeling a little unbalanced. If you're in a particularly tough fight (shout out, Death), a slippery whip or a weird platforming interaction is enough to end you. No matter how many of the stat-boosting trinkets you have equipped, no matter which of the seven weapon types you're using, you will be killed by a single misplaced boot on the edge of a ledge. That doesn't feel very Belmont.
Luckily, then, the pacing is great. Just when I'm starting to clutch my controller a bit too hard because I'm sick of hopping over spike traps and phasing between slabs of magical wall, Evil Empire seems to read my mind. 'Have at it, combat gauntlet!' it cries merrily, tossing a combination of enemies you've not yet encountered at you. 'I've got no health potions left!' you yelp, desperately. 'Good' the dev purrs. What follows is an exercise in pure desperation, a test of your savoir-faire, a reminder that for every boss you've purified so far, you've unlocked a new spell. Some of them refill your health - if you're canny about it. Others grant fleeting and precarious shields. More bind your enemies in one place, providing thankfully reliable anchors for your whip, allowing you to dash and hop over a sea of hazards taking over your screen.
In these moments, where the action-first philosophy of Evil Empire proudly puffs up its chest, and you make your own furniture to platform around, Belmont's Curse is exceptional. The Dead Cells DNA is undeniable, and the inspirations from decades of Castlevania glint off the flashes of your weapons as the blood of Night Creatures pools at your feet. The cortisol gives way to epinephrine, the acrobatics are tuned to assault. To use a fitting term, it gets your blood up.
Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a game of two halves; as well as the literal split that divides the Parisian sequences from the rest of the game, there's a spiritual cleve between its desire to be an action-platformer, and its aspirations of Metroidvania royalty. Like Rose herself, the game is earnest, intelligent, and capable of brilliance. But, mimicking its protagonist, it is also awkward, and unable to fully come to terms with its own unique identity in the shadow of its over-bearing legacy. By no means is Belmont's Curse a bad game, I just think Evil Empire sunk its teeth a bit too deep into something it wasn't quite ready to consume.
A copy of Castlevania: Belmont's Curse was provided for this review by Konami.

item.title: UPDATED 3.30PM BST: Dean Hall has explained more about his idea in an email exchange with Eurogamer, clarifying issues such as whether it uses or welcomes any form of generative AI, while offering some more strongly worded criticisms about Epic's Unreal engine and Unity. Read more
item.description:
UPDATED 3.30PM BST: Dean Hall has explained more about his idea in an email exchange with Eurogamer, clarifying issues such as whether it uses or welcomes any form of generative AI, while offering some more strongly worded criticisms about Epic's Unreal engine and Unity.
Primarily, I wanted to clarify what Brutal's relationship was with generative AI, if any, because it's the tech topic of the moment and something both Epic and Unreal, and Unity, are all-in on. In this regard, Hall answered: "There is no generative AI inside it, no tooling or scripts for making generative AI assets. Anyone can see for themselves as the repository is public. The framework is a tool for putting a game or engine together, not for generating anything."
Hall then tackled generative AI more broadly, particularly as it relates to Unreal and Unity, and said he finds it "confusing" that both engines focus "so much effort" on it. They are human-centric workflows, as he calls them - presumably meaning designed to be easily digestible by humans. "What, specifically, is it about Unreal - which has long focused on visual scripting, blueprints, and such - that would make it good for AI work?" He asked. "If we take all the promises as true, why would a human-centric workflow without the human be better than a language-centric workflow provided to a language model?"
I don't understand some of that but the "inconsistency" bothers Hall. "Let's take their arguments as gospel and say that AI is the way for them," he went on. "What happens when the cost of making those very tools yourself is approaching zero? Why pay to work around someone else's enormous, human-centric workflow when you can increasingly make the exact tools you need? The technology they're embracing might actually be undermining the very reason developers needed them in the first place."
It reminds him of the dot-com era "when companies tried to slap a coat of paint on themselves and suddenly become internet companies". "Unity and Unreal may be accelerating the adoption of the very technology that could undermine their business models," he said. "Pretty ironic."
Think about the control companies like Epic with Unreal, and Unity with its engine, have over a game developer's project, and what happens if they make a change or perhaps introduce a fee a developer is not happy with. What can the developer do? Because those are issues people face. "Is that going to get better?" Hall asked.
"And I want to be clear," he added, concluding. "I am not saying my Brutal framework is the winner." Instead, it's meant to be a start. "I want to say developers will tear down Unity and Unreal, but it is Unreal and Unity who are tearing themselves down. Their greed and lack of accountability to developers has left them completely unable to reconcile their need to appear relevant. They have to slap AI on everything while being an encumbrance for using the very thing they are pushing."
Incidentally, on the topic of Icarus using Unreal Engine 4: Hall and RocketWerkz have no plans to remove it. The studio has apparently "sunset" Unreal as an engine it uses but switching engine for Icarus would require a lot more work. "Migrating Icarus would be very disruptive," Hall said, "and our players are loyal and we've earned their trust through patches every single week for years now since launch, not missing one. An engine switch to Brutal would disrupt that."
ORIGINAL STORY 2PM BST: DayZ, Icarus, and Kitten Space Agency creator Dean Hall has issued a fiery assault against some of the world's biggest game companies, calling out a "greed" that's "rotting" our industry to its core. He took particular aim at engine-makers Epic (Unreal) and Unity, while simultaneously backing his words by launching an open-sourced, free alternative of his own: a game-making framework called Brutal.
"Our industry is rotting from its core," Hall wrote in an expansive post on Reddit, "outwards in every direction, and it has been for some time. Driven by greed, driven by a race to the bottom on price. It is my position that the games industry was already heading somewhere unsustainable before reverse-engineering and powerful agentic processes became widely available. These have pushed things over the edge.
"But I think one of the biggest problems is something we don't discuss enough. Developers have surrendered an extraordinary amount of control over their work to companies whose interests aren't necessarily aligned with their own. So we're doing something about it."
Brutal is a framework rather than a game engine, so it allows freedom to either make a game with it - as Hall's RocketWerkz studio has with Kitten Space Agency - or use another engine with it, like RimWorld's developer Ludeon has with its game engine Waylith.
"We're making the Brutal framework publicly available, with its source code, and we're making it free to use, including for commercial games, subject to an attribution requirement," Hall wrote. "There are no royalties and we don't want a percentage of your game's revenue."
Hall's post shares a lot of detail about the origins of Brutal, about what it is and who's working on it. He also admits and even underlines that Brutal won't be for everyone. "I do not believe this is the tool that everyone should use to make a game," Hall states. "We are not trying to make something that can do everything for everyone."
One particular anecdote that stands out to me is about where the spark came from to do this, and it sounds like it came from asking Epic boss Tim Sweeney a question during a Game Developers Conference 2025 talk.
"Tim was, for a long time, a hero of mine," Hall shared. "A powerhouse of a programmer with a mind I admired growing up. But over time I became frustrated with how much of the discussion seemed to revolve around the latest buzzwords. The metaverse one year, AI the next. Meanwhile developers were struggling with performance, stability, and the practical consequences of decisions made by engine vendors."
The question that Hall asked Sweeney about was whether Unreal was accountable to developers regarding those issues, to which Sweeney apparently replied something about "making more demos and putting them on social media to counter people describing games as 'Unreal slop'". Hall countered by asking whether making more things more quickly wasn't actually part of the problem, creating false expectations about how easy games are to make.
"I was not satisfied with his answer," Hall went on, "and I continue to believe Unreal is not accountable enough to developers. Particularly when it can take a five percent royalty on game revenue above its licensing threshold. I don't think developers should have to simply accept that relationship without questioning it."
Hall believes more frameworks like Brutal will emerge after this, not because everyone will "abandon" popular engines - Hall's Icarus uses Unreal Engine 4, incidentally - "but because the cost of making alternatives is going to fall dramatically". Brutal, he hopes, might provide developers a "lifeboat" to survive on.
"This technology is a small step towards changing the balance of power," Hall concluded. "If the tools are public, if you have the source code, and if you're free to build your own systems on top of them, you have options. And if one day we stop being accountable to developers ourselves, they should have the ability to fork the framework and go their own way. That's important to me. You are only as independent as your tools are. This is how we fight back."
I spoke at length with Dean Hall nearly a year ago, finding out how life had been for him more than a decade after leaving the project he's best known for - multiplayer survival shooter DayZ. The years have been fraught with ups and downs, with disorientation caused by success and then the many challenges faced running a studio of his own and navigating projects that don't immediately work out.
Icarus is a co-op survival crafting game that's been around for a few years on PC, but that launched on PS5 and Xbox Series S/X earlier this year. Kitten Space Agency, meanwhile, is an unashamed successor to Kerbal Space Agency, made by the creator of Kerbal, Felipe Falanghe. Kitten Space Agency was released in pre-alpha for free last autumn, via RocketWerkz' own distribution platform Ahwoo, with an optional donation business model - another of Hall's experiments. And it's raised more than $230,000 so far that way.

item.title: League of Legends Classic, the recreation of an older version of the popular MOBA, will be taken down at the end of the current season. The reason given is simple: most players have moved on to other areas of League of Legends. Read more
item.description:
League of Legends Classic, the recreation of an older version of the popular MOBA, will be taken down at the end of the current season. The reason given is simple: most players have moved on to other areas of League of Legends.
First released in July this year, LoL Classic was implied to have potential as a permanent addition, though such aspirations seems to have swiftly ended. Instead, it'll be taken offline next January, with a planned return likely as a limited-time mode in the future with ample changes.
In an official blog post by Riot Games, the League team writes: "We've seen a lot of players have fun revisiting the olden days with Classic. At this point though, most have gone back to other parts of League. So Classic will be available through the rest of Season 3 and will then end its current run in January 2027. We’ll then put Classic back in the box for now, with the goal of bringing it back, likely as an event mode with adjustments and additions.
"There's more we're going to share in the future about what we learned from this run. That includes where we think we got Classic right, where we could have gone more classic, and where sticking too closely to the past may have held the experience back. Please continue to let us know what you love and don't love about Classic. Your feedback is a vital part of how we make our games and is always appreciated."
Those who had bought cosmetic microtransactions for LoL Classic will have them refunded in Riot Points premium currency. Planned Classic champions, including Volibear, Urgot, and Udyr, will still release as planned. There's no word on exactly when LoL Classic will return following its closure, and what changes the team has in mind for a new iteration.
League of Legends Classic was initially met with excitement from longtime LoL lovers, though the game mode was met with controversy due to its microtransaction model. While champions did possess their older move set, obtaining the retro look required players to either earn them through a Classic-specific battle pass or buy them with real world moolah. Many found charging for Classic skins in a Classic game mode was a step too far.
While League Classic fans may be saddened by the news that the mode will soon be taken away, the silver lining here is that the proposed return of League Classic could provide a better experience that enraptures a larger portion of the playerbase for longer. Fingers crossed the next attempt comes back in a big way.

item.title: The Switch 2 version of 007 First Light will be released 18th March, 2027, IO Interactive has announced. The game had originally been expected this summer but IOI announced a delay to an unspecific date in March roughly a month ago. Read more
item.description:
The Switch 2 version of 007 First Light will be released 18th March, 2027, IO Interactive has announced. The game had originally been expected this summer but IOI announced a delay to an unspecific date in March roughly a month ago.
"Since announcing additional development time to ensure the quality of experience players expect, IO Interactive has brought hands-on builds of 007 First Light to both gamescom and Tokyo Game Show, where players and press had their first opportunity to experience Bond's world running on Nintendo's hardware," the company said in a press release statement.
"Player response from both events has been positive, reflecting the progress being made across the game as development continues toward launch. The development team will use the coming months to continue refining the game's optimisation and performance on Nintendo Switch 2, ensuring it meets the standard players expect at launch."
Evidently, it hasn't been a smooth transition. We've heard similar things from Capcom, for what it's worth, with the Monster Hunter Wilds devs claiming it was a "painstaking, seemingly endless process" to get the game running well on Switch 2.
The date announcement coincides with pre-orders of a Deluxe Edition going live, which offers access to some extra clothes and gadgets in game. We're also only a couple of weeks on from 007 First Light getting a bumper blob of add-on content, in the form of New Game Plus, a new, harder difficulty, a photo mode, more replayable TacSim challenge missions, and a bit of general game tuning. Presumably all of this will be included in the Switch 2 version when it launches.
As it stands, 007 First Light has been one of the stand-out successes of 2026, bringing James Bond back to gaming with flair and aplomb. The Hitman studio delivered a tight, exciting, cinematic single-player adventure filled with charm and wit - not unlike James Bond himself. Eurogamer's gleaming 007 First Light review can tell you more.
The game also appears to have been a commercial success, having passed 4 million sales since release - and with a Switch 2 version to come, there's more selling to do. I imagine it makes the likelihood of a sequel very strong, though newish Bond franchise owner Amazon has said it wants to be involved in whatever comes next, whereas IOI was the master of its own destiny with 007 First Light.
Meanwhile, IOI is also making a fantasy game called, well, Project Fantasy. This was announced as an online RPG in 2023, but faced a major setback recently when publisher Xbox pulled out of the project, forcing IOI to close one of its studios and make layoffs across the company - even in the aftermath of 007 First LIght's success. IOI has since regained full ownership of the game and has vowed to continue to develop Project Fantasy independently.
The studio also continues to develop and expand Hitman World of Assassination, which recently added rapper Snoop Dogg as an elusive target.

item.description:
Big Walk developer House House has explained the lack of an Xbox version for the popular co-operative puzzle game, pointing to the ongoing BDS boycott as the core reason behind its decision.

This decision means that some people will miss out on playing Big Walk with their friends, and we understand the disappointment we’re causing. We are disappointed too.
"We would love for people to be able to play the game on Xbox, but not until Microsoft and/or Xbox have been removed as BDS boycott targets.
"We’ve made this decision with the belief that meaningful change can be made in the world, that coordinated collective action can confront even the most powerful interests, and that one day, Palestine will be free."
The Palestinian-led BDS movement has been a staunch proponent of various boycotts aimed at companies who have supported Israel's government during the genocide in Palistine. It has published a list of boycott targets, which includes Disney, Intel, and Xbox.
Xbox's inclusion on the list is due to Microsoft's partnership with Israel and its prison system according to BDS. The company has provided the country use of its Azure Cloud and AI systems, which have been used consistently over the past few years in the ongoing subjugation of Palestinians. BDS has urged people to cancel their Game Pass subscriptions, boycott major franchises including Call of Duty and Candy Crush, and cease purchases of Microsoft gaming products.
Big Walk, despite its lack of an Xbox version, has proven quite popular. A game of great merit, the game sold over one million copies in under a week following its release on the 4th August.

item.title: Capcom is letting players 'try before they buy' Monster Hunter Wilds' on Switch 2, bringing the fairly generous 'Prologue demo' to the console before the game's full release on the platform on 4th December. Read more
item.description:
Capcom is letting players 'try before they buy' Monster Hunter Wilds' on Switch 2, bringing the fairly generous 'Prologue demo' to the console before the game's full release on the platform on 4th December.
The demo, which arrives on 19th October, lets you play the very beginning of the game up to the beginning of Chapter 1-3,"To the Forest". It's offline-only, so you don't get to experience the full joy of four-player hunts - but you do at least get to try out all 14 weapon types, and get full access to the character creator. Also, your save data will migrate from the demo to the full game, similarly to how the demo pathing works on PC and other consoles.
Unlike other consoles, though, there is an option to play local multiplayer with the demo. This means if someone else nearby has the demo downloaded on their Switch 2, you'll be able to play with them - trying out some of the hunts in co-op (honestly, that is how the game is meant to be played, if you ask me). There has been quite a lot of speculation about how a game as massive as Monster Hunter Wilds - complete with all the controversy we saw about its performance over the year it launched - will run on Switch 2, so it's pretty neat that Capcom is giving you a chance to try it out for yourself.
For my money, a lot of the initial criticisms of Monster Hunter Wilds have been addressed since its shaky launch; Capcom has been fastidious in making sure the difficulty complaints were taken care of, and performance has been steadily enhanced, patch after patch. In fact, the developer even noted how the Switch 2 version of the game actually helped improve all the other versions, remarking on the "painstaking, seemingly endless process" it took to get the game in a shippable state on the hybrid console.
The Switch 2 release of the game represents another step on Capcom's journey towards making Wilds more popular than the esteemed Worlds - the publisher's end goal is "surpassing" the dizzying apex of Monster Hunter World's sales and popularity. To this end, it seems Capcom has all hands on deck with the upcoming expansion, Ascendance, something we're hoping to see more of in due course.

item.description:
UPDATE 21:37pm UK: In a follow-up tweet, Uchikoshi clarified that he's still part of TooKyo Games and he hasn't fallen out with fellow studio co-founder Kazutaka Kodaka. In fact, Kodaka jokes he "may have fallen in love" with the Danganronpa dev. "We're still so close that we even have pajama parties at each other's houses, sipping strawberry milk boba together."
As for his new studio's cancelled game - which you can read about below - it's no surprise to hear that Uchikoshi can't get into the finer details of why it got scrapped or what he was actually making. "I'll let you use your imagination, but if Uchi fans had heard the title, they might have danced like crazy with nosebleeds for three days and three nights straight," he wrote. "On a more serious note, I think it's fair to say that major changes in the game development landscape may have played a part. And what brought about those changes? Needless to say... AI (artificial intelligence)."
The famed Zero Escape writer explained that gen-AI has put somewhat of a squeeze on "mid-sized developers" who need to find ways of lowering the cost of making games - particularly pertinent this week as Google announced a publicly available gen-AI game dev tool. Here's what Uchikoshi had to say about the topic:
"Advances in AI have made it possible for people to create games at a much lower cost. To stay competitive, mid-sized game developers like us need to find ways to cut costs. However, these days, using AI to make games is generally frowned upon, isn't it? Unfortunately, under these circumstances, we're fighting a losing battle.
"It's often assumed that using AI could cause creators to lose their jobs. But the opposite can also be true. In other words, "not using AI" could also cause creators to lose their jobs. If using AI had been an option, perhaps the project wouldn't have been canceled. Of course, humans would have handled all the creative work, leaving only the tedious tasks to AI. That way, we might have been able to cut development time, not staff.
"Oh, and just to be clear, that doesn't mean the budget was the direct cause of the cancellation. I'm just saying that if we'd been able to cut costs further, things might have turned out differently."
ORIGINAL STORY 20:14pm UK:A new game from Kotaro Uchikoshi (of Zero Escape and The Hundred Line: Last Defense Academy fame) has been cancelled, leaving his studio's fate in doubt.
Uchikoshi first became a beloved name after he wrote and directed the Zero Escape trilogy, a cult classic series of locked-room puzzlers on the DS that was eventually ported to modern platforms. The self-proclaimed "Deadass Underrated Director" recently jumped online both to announce his new studio Crash Keys and ask for help.
"Honestly, I'm not doing well at all... Why, you ask...? Because the game our whole team had poured our hearts and souls into for about a year and a half was suddenly canceled," he tweeted earlier today. "I mean, I lost my job overnight. Talk about a bolt from the blue."
Crash Keys actually opened its doors in March 2025, and Uchikoshi planned to formally reveal the company and its first game sometime next year. "But then came that whole 'bolt from the blue' incident," he explained - forcing him to go public earlier than expected.
The studio is now looking for anyone who "might be interested in working with us or investing in our projects." In his typical off-key humour, Uchikoshi warned the developer might struggle to stay afloat without some kind of investment. "Please give us some work! At this rate, our company might literally crash into a million pieces. My team and I may be forced to survive on nothing but cicada shells collected from a run-down park. So please, help us! You're our only hope!"
The Crash Keys website only lists two other employees. There's Akira Mine, a writer with credits on Hundred Line and the upcoming Danganronpa 2x2, and Muri Sasaki, who contributed to both Zero Escape and AI: The Somnium Files. As some players have noted, Crash Keys also happens to be the name of a very important organisation in the Zero Escape trilogy, which raised a few eyebrows from starving series fans online.
After wrapping up work on the Zero Escape series, Uchikoshi co-founded a different development company (TooKyo Games) alongside another beloved visual novel maker - Danganronpa's Kazutaka Kodaka. The pair released the wildly ambitious but criminally overlooked strategy game The Hundred Line last year. It's unclear if Uchikoshi is still involved with TooKyo currently.

item.title: Epic Games isn't lifting its foot off the gen-AI pedal. The company behind Fortnite and Unreal Engine has now vibe-coded a new Epic Games Launcher in an attempt to outrun Steam, by far the most popular digital games marketplace on PC. Read more
item.description:
Epic Games isn't lifting its foot off the gen-AI pedal. The company behind Fortnite and Unreal Engine has now vibe-coded a new Epic Games Launcher in an attempt to outrun Steam, by far the most popular digital games marketplace on PC.
The Epic Games Launcher is the platform that grants players access to the Epic Games Store, their game libraries and a host of social features - and the app's newest version was prompted into existence with the use of generative AI, according to the company.
"We vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy," Epic tweeted alongside a graph (below) comparing how much faster the EGS Launcher is to boot than Steam (Five seconds!) "Is this bad boy faster? Yes. Will it have some bugs? Yes. Do we want to hear about them? Hell yes. When you find something that’s off, hit the 'Send Feedback' button in the Launcher so we can tackle on the road to release."
We vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy. Don't believe us? Test it out for yourself in Preview: https://t.co/pdtAeEIri4 https://t.co/aMxojUUVPV
A follow-up blog post attempts to justify the gen-AI usage: "Programming is hard. So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that's way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look. The first release is light on features. Think of it as a speedboat and not a yacht!" (Is that more Valve shade I see?)
Vibe coding is a colloquial term often used to refer to code generated or prompted with gen-AI. Speaking to IGN, EGS' vice president and general manager Martin Keely acknowledged it's an "issue that's of high visibility" across the games industry at the moment - countless games have been recompiled and decompiled in recent weeks by vibe coders - but Keely reckons it's "made us more efficient and allowed a small team to rewrite the code base and be able to launch it faster across platforms."
This comes just a day after a Bloomberg report claimed Epic Games is fully embracing an "AI first" development pipeline, starting with a Marvel and Star Wars shooter that was internally delayed. Developers were allegedly told that "no more hand-written code" should be used while making the Disney crossover project from here on, and even art should be "generated with full AI workflows".
In an online post, CEO Tim Sweeney also suggested the gen-AI pivot could seep into Unreal Engine, the widely-used game development tool behind everything from Gears of War: E-Day to Final Fantasy 7 Revelation: "The aim isn't to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build more and better stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal."
The Epic Games Store has long struggled to pull the vast majority of PC players away from Valve's Steam platform. We'll see if a controversial AI spin can move the needle in any way.
